docs.title: Does a massive remnant migrate like a test particle? (friction test, tails/friction_test.py)
docs.text:
Class-3 back-integration with Chandrasekhar friction for a constant bound mass (100 samples, vectorised leapfrog in the time-dependent AGAMA potential; nucleus-mass drift 11 kpc km/s/Gyr matches the paper's 9.6). Fraction inside GSE 8 Gyr ago:

Ω_b,0 20 21 22 22.5 23 24 25 26 27 test particle 0.44 0.38 0.58 0.85 0.01 0.89 0.79 0.18 0.00 M = 10⁷ 0.81 0.55 0.77 0.02 0.89 0.93 0.98 0.64 0.03 M = 10⁸ 0.00 0.07 0.47 0.15 0.44 0.34 0.00 0.00 0.00 M = 10⁹ — — — — — 0.00 (apo 79 kpc) — — —

The response changes substantially between the 10⁷ and 10⁸ M☉ trials, but also depends strongly on pattern speed: even the 10⁷-M☉ row has a dip to 0.02 at 22.5. At 24, the 10⁸-M☉ fraction is 0.34, not zero. These results suggest substantial envelope loss before bar migration; they do not establish a universal ≲10⁸-M☉ bound. A constant-mass trial can overstate or understate the cumulative drag of a real history depending on which mass it represents. Endpoint membership in the GSE contour is a diagnostic, not itself a demonstration of capture. Numbers are from the unit-corrected reruns of 2026-09-20. Figure: plots/friction_test_elz.png; tables: results/tails/friction_test.ecsv and friction_test_grid.ecsv.

docs.title: What is still not modelled
docs.text:
• Anything before the bar formed (> 8 Gyr ago): GSE's own infall and disruption (Naidu et al. 2021 fiducial: M★ = 5 × 10⁸, M_DM = 2 × 10¹¹, from R_vir at z ≈ 2, circularity 0.5, retrograde) and where ω Cen's host sat in it. The two readings of "deposited by GSE" (ω Cen = GSE's nucleus; or a smaller host in group infall) both start from the picked debris orbit.
  • A self-consistent mass-loss/friction history. Class 2 prescribes mass loss; the class-3 friction tests use fixed masses. Neither evolves a live host and remnant together.
  • The bar-history caveat recorded in the oCen_bar journal: with fixed η = 0.003 a present-day Ω_b,0 = 35 implies an initial Ω₁ = 110 km/s/kpc, so the scan over Ω_b,0 is also a scan over implausible early histories; the low-Ω_b,0 requirement is tied to this slowdown law.

docs.title: What differs between the classes (for the simulations)
docs.text: early orbit (≥ 5 Gyr ago) late orbit pericentre class 1 today's today's 1.3–2.0 kpc class 2 wider, apo 10–20 kpc at 5 Gyr, infall from R_vir today's 1.6–2.9 kpc early class 3 most-bound GSE debris, apo 11–12 kpc, L_z ≈ 0 to +230, until ~2.5 Gyr ago today's, reached by bar migration in the last ~2.5 Gyr 0.4–0.45 kpc (0.8 in the barred potential today)

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Chandrasekhar friction with σ = v_c/√2 and a fixed r_h is a 20–30% level approximation; the mass-history dependence is far larger than that.
  • Only McMillan 2017 for class 2 (AGAMA host); class 3 uses Hunter et al. 2024 (the only potential with the fitted bar); class 1 carries the potential spread.
  • The galpy ChandrasekharDynamicalFrictionForce (Python force, ~30 min per orbit) is kept as class2_friction_backwards for cross-checks; the fast leapfrog is the working tool.
  • galpy checkout at <src>/galpy is from 2024-03 and needs two import shims (astroquery metadata, scipy vectorize1), both in progenitor_orbits._import_galpy_safely.

docs.title: Compact DF implementation and numerical tests
docs.text:
Historical (2026-09)

Written before the central point mass was added. Since commit 9d600ae (2026-10-15) the DF supports an exact central point mass; see the dated update after the alpha>1/2 paragraph below and kb/models/df_bh.md. Current fitted models: kb/models/base_no_dm.md.

The compact stellar model is implemented in regularized_df.py. The independent generalized lowered-isothermal control is implemented in lowered_isothermal.py. Both predict the same surface-density and three projected second-moment quantities used by the existing binned likelihood. Existing DoublePowerLaw models and saved configurations keep their original interpretation.

docs.title: Regularized stellar family
docs.text:
The stellar DF is

\[ f=A\exp[-(L_c/J_0)^\alpha],\qquad b(q)=b_{\rm out}\frac{q^2}{q^2+J_a^2},\quad q=J_r+L. \]

The default model has five stellar coordinates: mass, action scale, envelope index, anisotropy amplitude and transition action. An optional second transition adds an outer amplitude and a larger transition action. Neither amplitude is identified with the velocity-moment anisotropy beta(r).

The code follows constant-DF contours in log(q) and c=L/q. It tabulates their circular endpoints and uses a cubic interpolation whose radial boundary preserves f_Jr/f_L=2. Action-space quadrature includes the signed-Jphi volume factor and checks its normalization by doubling the integration order. DF evaluation is positive by construction; no negative-value clipping is used. Unbound phase-space points return zero.

The exact spherical orbital-frequency reference is the default. AGAMA maps actions to an orbit, then its direct action/frequency integrator supplies Omega_r/Omega_t. Direct integration avoids a regression case in which the interpolated Hamiltonian derivative becomes negative on a very eccentric, weakly bound orbit. The analytic radial limit is used at L=0, and the circular epicycle limit at Jr/L<1e-5 avoids singular period integrals when the turning points coincide. The latter has an error of order Jr/L. This local numerical limit is distinct from the optional global frequency_mode="epicycle" approximation. That approximation is retained for comparison, not adopted as an exactly isotropic model.

Frequency evaluation uses an equatorial representative with Jz=0 and Jphi=L. Spherical symmetry preserves Jr, L, and the frequencies while avoiding a polar coordinate singularity in the native action mapper. The preserved failure and regression document the issue found during the first recovery smoke test.

Every self-gravity iteration rebuilds the contour map and its normalization in the updated total potential. The final density is checked between radial grid points with twice the velocity quadrature. Convergence includes stellar density as well as total force, so a dominant halo cannot conceal an unconverged tracer. Relative density closure is measured where density exceeds 1e-12 of its peak or stellar mass per log-radius exceeds 1e-8 of Mstar. Only the negligible numerical tail below 1e-30 of the peak is continued for logarithmic density/moment interpolation. Its contribution is included in the independent stellar mass-closure check; the DF itself is not floored.

The implementation requires alpha>1/2. In a harmonic core at r=0, Lc is proportional to v^2, so f(v)-f(0) is proportional to |v|^(2 alpha). This bound makes its first velocity derivative tend to zero at the origin. Finite normalization alone would require only alpha>0. Central black holes are not supported by this finite-central-potential prescription.

Update (2026-10-15, commit 9d600ae): an exact central point mass is now supported (PrescribedMatter.M_bh, default 0, added to the potential as a zero-radius Plummer sphere). With a point mass the radial-orbit limit of f_Jr/f_L is 1 instead of 2 (the boundary statement above holds for a finite centre only), and eccentric orbits around it use exact apsidal-angle quadrature instead of AGAMA frequencies. M_bh = 0 reproduces the base fit exactly. Fits: kb/models/df_bh.md.

docs.title: Prescribed dark densities
docs.text:
The halo uses the exact coordinate rho20=rho_DM(20 pc), a scale radius, and either gamma=0 or gamma=1 as separate families. Its outer taper is exp[-(r/r_t)^2], normalized at 20 pc along with the inner profile. The taper radius is fixed in the supplied examples. This is deliberately a new density implementation: the older Jeans/DF templates use a different taper, and are unchanged. No-DM is a separate model with rho20=0. The optional remnant density is Plummer with its own mass and radius.

The dark components enter Poisson gravity without dark orbital parameters. This constructs a positive equilibrium stellar DF. It does not establish phase-space admissibility of the prescribed halo/remnant densities, dynamical stability or survival in the Galactic tidal field.

docs.title: Independent lowered-isothermal control
docs.text:
The control implements

\[ f(E,L)=A\exp[-L^2/(2r_a^2s^2)] E_\gamma(g,(E_t-E)/s^2),\qquad E<E_t, \]

and zero otherwise. This is the generalized Michie/LIMEPY family, implemented with direct velocity quadrature and an embedded spherical Poisson solve. It does not call the external LIMEPY package, and it is not the Osipkov-Merritt energy-shift mock in df_mock.py.

The five stellar controls are central dimensionless depth W0, velocity scale, central stellar density, anisotropy radius and truncation index. Stellar mass, DF amplitude and energy cutoff follow from the solution. Dark gravity enters the Poisson integration itself. Tests compare the isotropic King limit to the independent existing mock solver and check Jeans balance in embedded cored and cusped halos. The supplied examples have finite anisotropy radii; a large fixed radius supplies an explicitly isotropic control.

docs.title: Running and reproducing the checks
docs.text:
All commands below use the project virtual environment and one numerical thread. They create fresh result directories; they do not launch posterior sampling.

PYTHONPATH=src OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MPLCONFIGDIR=/tmp/ocen-df-mpl \
  python -m pytest \
  tests/test_regularized_df.py tests/test_lowered_isothermal.py \
  tests/test_positive_df.py tests/test_df_capacity.py tests/test_df_mass_recovery.py -q

python \
  bin/validate_regularized_df.py --out results/diagnostics/CHOOSE_A_FRESH_NAME

The validation driver records source copies and hashes, analytical checks, constant-DF contour accuracy, self-consistency, independent projections and Jeans balance, different starting potentials, doubled numerical grids and the numerical shift in the actual saved observational bins. Its JSON report and iteration log live in the chosen result directory. PNGs go to plots/; their arrays and provenance go to results/plot_data/.

Six unfitted starting specifications are in configs/df/: the regularized_* and lowered_isothermal_* files, each with no-DM, cored and cusped variants. Their fit bounds are explicit optimizer bounds, not adopted probability priors. The existing bin/run_df_pilot.py accepts either family through its usual --config argument. Light normalization remains a profiled photometric zero point in this diagnostic likelihood. The driver preserves data snapshots and stores the new source files with each run.

docs.title: Scope of the present validation
docs.text:
These checks establish numerical implementation and representative equilibria. They do not establish that the compact family fits Omega Cen or can recover dark density without bias. Matched and independent mock recovery, prior and outer-taper sensitivity, tracer-selection/equipartition checks, and subsequent rotation/flattening tests remain separate research stages.

The next stage is the matched-family compact DF recovery experiment, with noiseless no-DM and injected-halo mocks, two starting points, and separate checks of numerical accuracy, observable residuals, and physical mass recovery.

docs.title: Rung 0: analysis of the three isotropic fits
docs.text:
Historical (2026-09)

Superseded by kb/models/jeans_comparison.md and kb/models/dm_fits.md.

2026-09-21. Runs rung0_K1, rung0_K2_cored, rung0_K2_nfw in results/fits/; comparison table results/fits/comparison.md; figures plots/fit_posterior_profiles.png, plots/fit_rung0_*_posterior_profiles.png. Plan: docs/MODELLING_PLAN.md; data: docs/data_analysis.pdf; method: docs/mass_modelling.pdf.

Baseline stage complete (2026-09-21). These runs establish the intended reference for the next modelling steps. All three saved maximum-likelihood values reproduce exactly with the current code and data. Their residuals guide tests of anisotropy, rotation and other extensions. No new posterior was sampled during the audit or subsequent reporting repairs; see CODE_ANALYSIS_AUDIT.md.

docs.title: 1. What was run
docs.text:
Rung 0 of the ladder: the simplest defensible model. Isotropic (β ≡ 0), no instrument scale factors, composite tracer, our own Jeans solver, 89 binned points:

dataset points radial range hst_pm_radial_ours 21 3.7–342″ (0.1–8.8 pc) hst_pm_tangential_ours 21 3.7–342″ muse_los_dispersion 29 5.7–290″ gaia_edr3_ours_radial 9 357–2149″ (9.2–55 pc) gaia_edr3_ours_tangential 9 357–2149″

Switches recorded in run.yaml: gaia_errors: raw, gaia_rotation: published, isotropic: true, no_scales: true. Three families: K1 (stars + remnants + point mass, 5 parameters), K2-cored and K2-NFW (K1 plus a two-parameter halo, M_dm_100 and r_s).

docs.title: 2. Results
docs.text:
K1 (no DM) K2 cored K2 NFW ln Z −190.02 ± 0.48 −188.94 ± 0.36 −190.09 ± 0.35 max ln L −169.7 −164.4 −165.5 χ² at max L (89 points) 772 761 763 M★ [M☉] 2.88 [2.67, 3.03] ×10⁶ 2.30 [1.68, 2.77] ×10⁶ 2.34 [1.57, 2.85] ×10⁶ M_rem [M☉] 3.1 [2.0, 4.8] ×10⁵ 7.7 [3.9, 13.3] ×10⁵ 7.1 [3.2, 13.4] ×10⁵ a_rem [pc] 4.0 [3.2, 4.7] 5.2 [4.3, 5.7] 5.1 [4.1, 5.7] M_BH [M☉] 4.34 [3.90, 4.71] ×10⁴ 4.65 [4.29, 4.97] ×10⁴ 4.53 [4.11, 4.88] ×10⁴ M_DM(<100 pc) [M☉] — 1.32 [0.19, 2.47] ×10⁶ 5.3 [0.23, 11.9] ×10⁵ r_s [pc] — 261 [46, 663] 123 [7, 544] D [kpc] 5.311 [5.291, 5.332] 5.312 [5.291, 5.333] 5.313 [5.292, 5.334] 95 % upper limit M_DM(<100 pc) — 3.13 ×10⁶ 1.64 ×10⁶ likelihood calls / wall time 3.2 ×10⁶ / 4.0 h 6.6 ×10⁶ / 10.0 h 14.3 ×10⁶ / 20.6 h

Δ ln Z: cored − K1 = +1.08 ± 0.60; NFW − K1 = −0.08 ± 0.59; cored − NFW = +1.16 ± 0.50. The cored-to-K1 Bayes factor is about 2.9. Neither halo family is persuasively preferred within this baseline. Because all three models fit poorly, these evidence differences cannot establish the physical presence or absence of a halo.

Input-hash discrepancy. The report flags the runs because the Gaia product's hash changed between launches. Re-evaluating the three saved best samples now reproduces their stored log likelihoods exactly and all per-dataset χ² values to their recorded precision. This supports the journal's interpretation of a metadata-only change. It is not a proof that every original likelihood input was identical: the run directories do not contain immutable copies of the fitted arrays. The report warning is retained. Launch-time hashes now reduce this risk, but do not freeze inputs or cover the tracer source files.

docs.title: 3. Goodness of fit: the excess χ² is concentrated beyond 50″
docs.text:
χ² at the K2-cored maximum-likelihood point, split by projected radius:

dataset R < 50″ 50–150″ > 150″ HST radial 12.9 (11 pts, 1.2/pt) 49.5 (5) 90.1 (5) HST tangential 13.6 (11 pts, 1.2/pt) 165.8 (5) 304.4 (5, 61/pt) MUSE LOS 9.5 (13 pts, 0.7/pt) 27.5 (10) 38.9 (6)

Inside 50″ the residuals are consistent with the adopted uncertainties. Most of the excess χ² comes from larger radii; HST tangential contributes 484 of the total 761.

The misfit is small in physical terms. Fractional residuals (data − model)/data:

108″ 138″ 176″ 224″ 271″ 311″ HST radial +0.3 % +1.4 % +1.2 % +1.1 % +0.2 % −1.2 % HST tangential −2.0 % −3.7 % −5.1 % −7.5 % −9.6 % −10.0 % statistical error 0.26–0.30 % 0.24–0.35 % 0.20–0.49 % 0.16–0.79 % 0.21–1.19 % 0.51–1.61 %

χ² = 761 corresponds to a model wrong by 1 % in one component and 5–10 % in another. It looks catastrophic only because the HST errors are 0.16–0.35 % in those bins. The fit errors also include propagated rotation uncertainty where applicable; the table shows statistical errors alone. The large χ² establishes model/data tension. Missing anisotropy and calibration or selection effects are possible causes, and mass estimates can remain biased until those causes are tested.

docs.title: 4. Component ratios motivate anisotropy tests
docs.text:
The geometric mean of the two PM components is matched to 2–3 % at 150–300″, while their ratio has a stronger radial residual. Matching that mean is not an independent measurement of enclosed mass: projection, tracer density, anisotropy and streaming also enter. The isotropic model does not predict exactly 1 for this ratio, because the tangential model has the published rotation subtracted; the residual excess (data ratio over model ratio) is the part that needs new physics:

R 2.2 pc 3.6 pc 5.8 pc 8.0 pc 9.2 pc 13.7 pc 21.4 pc 26.9 pc 34.2 pc 43.6 pc 55.3 pc data σ_T/σ_R 0.979 0.937 0.881 0.847 0.931 0.859 0.940 0.988 1.081 1.103 1.176 model σ_T/σ_R 0.995 0.985 0.958 0.920 0.901 0.850 0.907 0.939 0.967 0.989 0.998 excess −1.6 % −4.8 % −8.0 % −8.0 % +3.3 % +1.1 % +3.6 % +5.3 % +11.8 % +11.6 % +17.9 %

(The first four columns are HST, the rest Gaia EDR3; 9.2 pc onwards is a different instrument, so the step at 8 → 9 pc should not be over-interpreted.)

This pattern is consistent with radial anisotropy at intermediate radii and tangential anisotropy farther out, as expected if tides preferentially remove radial orbits. The projected ratios do not directly recover intrinsic β(r), and the radii are projected. Within Gaia alone, the measured ratio rises from 0.86 near 11 pc to 1.18 near 55 pc, crossing unity around 27 pc. That observation motivates a turnover model; it does not uniquely determine one.

MUSE is also below the isotropic prediction at large projected radius (9.4% at 290″). Its response to radial anisotropy makes this a useful independent-instrument check. Different tracer populations and the approximate rotation treatment remain alternatives.

docs.title: The alternative reading
docs.text: The tangential component is also where rotation enters, so an error in the rotation curve produces the same signature. Quantitatively: reconciling the HST tangential data at 224″ requires an extra 5.8 km/s in quadrature on top of the 4.45 km/s the published curve already supplies there, i.e. a ~64 % larger rotation amplitude at 5.8 pc; and reconciling the outer Gaia points requires less rotation than the model subtracts at 34–55 pc. A single normalisation error cannot do both — it would need the shape of the rotation curve to be wrong in opposite directions at 6 and 40 pc. This makes a common amplitude error an incomplete explanation. Test the Gaia alternative with --gaia-rotation ours; there is no equivalent HST switch. HST needs an external absolute rotation estimate because local corrections removed its streaming. Reports now replay saved Gaia options and check the stored likelihood. Anisotropy and rotation errors can coexist.

docs.title: 5. Error-floor sensitivity at the existing best sample
docs.text:
χ² at the same best model with a systematic floor added in quadrature (not refitted):

floor 0 0.5 % 1 % 2 % HST radial 152 38 19 11 HST tangential 484 272 149 63 MUSE 76 72 62 42 Gaia radial 25 24 19 12 Gaia tangential 24 23 21 16 total (89) 761 428 271 144

A 0.5 % floor fixes the HST radial component almost completely (152 → 38): that misfit really is error-bar-driven. The tangential component is not: it still contributes 63 of the 144 at a 2 % floor. The structured residual remains. This calculation does not refit the model and therefore does not rule out every alternative error model. --gaia-errors eta changes the Gaia measurements; it does not add an HST systematic floor or directly address this HST pattern.

docs.title: 6. What the "evidence for dark matter" is actually made of
docs.text:
Δχ² between K1 and K2-cored, by dataset:

HST radial HST tangential MUSE Gaia radial Gaia tangential total Δχ² (K2-cored − K1) −8 +7 −1 +6 −14 −10

The halo buys Δχ² ≈ 10 for two parameters, and the gain comes almost entirely from the outer Gaia points: the tangential ones improve by 14 and the radial ones worsen by 6. Those are the same 34–55 pc points that demand β < 0. An isotropic model can only raise both components together, and raising them helps the tangential data (which sit above the model) more than it hurts the radial data (which sit below). The improvement is consistent with the halo compensating for missing outer tangential anisotropy. That mechanism needs a fit with the additional orbital freedom to establish it. The evidence difference of +1.1 is insufficient for a DM claim.

docs.title: 7. Other parameters
docs.text:
Distance. All three runs give D = 5.311–5.313 ± 0.021 kpc against a prior of 5.43 ± 0.05 — the data pull it down by 2.4 prior σ and tighten it by a factor 2.4. This is a kinematic distance from matching proper motions in mas/yr to line-of-sight velocities in km/s, and it is driven mainly by the inner data where the fit is good. It is nevertheless a result that should be re-checked at rung 1, because anisotropy changes the PM-to-LOS ratio and so can bias D.

Central mass. The total M★ + M_rem + M_BH is 3.23 ×10⁶ (K1) and 3.12 ×10⁶ (K2-cored), i.e. stable, but the split moves a lot: adding a halo moves 6 ×10⁵ M☉ from the stars to the remnants. M_BH is 4.3–4.7 ×10⁴ M☉ with an 8 % error in all three runs; the inner fit is good (χ²/point = 1.2), but this does not make the point-mass estimate robust. The central mass–anisotropy degeneracy is untested. Moreover, an exactly cored tracer in a central point-mass potential requires β(0) ≤ −1/2 for a non-negative DF; the isotropic moment baseline violates that necessary condition in the central limit.

Halo parameters. r_s is unconstrained in both K2 runs (46–663 pc cored, 7–544 pc NFW), which is expected: the data end at 55 pc and the halo is a small perturbation there.

docs.title: 8. Independent-engine check
docs.text:
Evaluating each best sample with JamPy instead of our Jeans solver:

run our solver JamPy K1 ln L = −169.66 −170.35 K2-cored −164.44 −165.08

The total log likelihoods differ by about 0.7. Individual HST χ² terms shift by roughly 18 and largely cancel; the other terms shift by less than 1. The engines share the intended spherical moment equations, but JamPy uses an MGE approximation to non-Gaussian mass components and independent numerical integration. This audit has not isolated the cause of the residual difference. Total-likelihood agreement alone is not a per-component accuracy certificate.

docs.title: 9. Sampling cost
docs.text: K1 took 4 h and 3.2 ×10⁶ likelihood calls; K2-cored 10 h / 6.6 ×10⁶; K2-NFW 20.6 h / 14.3 ×10⁶. The NFW run spent most of its time crawling along the M_DM–r_s degeneracy ridge (one accepted draw per ~4000 calls for several hours, with 82 % of the evidence still in the live points after 12 h). For rungs 1 and 2, which add one and three parameters, the NFW family should test UltraNest's step sampler (--step-sampler) and check convergence. A prior change requires scientific justification and changes the evidence; it is not a numerical substitute for improving sampling.

docs.title: 10. Conclusions and next experiments
docs.text:
1. All three isotropic models have acceptable central residuals and a poor outer fit.
  2. The strongest residual is in the relative PM components. It motivates radial variation in anisotropy, but does not independently certify the mass profile.
  3. A model with intermediate radial and outer tangential anisotropy is a testable interpretation. Rotation, tracer selection and correlated errors remain relevant.
  4. The small cored-halo preference may compensate for missing orbital freedom. It is not a DM detection; retain the table's limits only as conditional baseline outputs.

Follow MODELLING_PLAN.md: constant-β controls first, then a specified turnover extension. The existing three-parameter β(r) is monotonic and is not the proposed turnover model. Neither rung 1 nor the extension has yet superseded these runs with a completed current-data posterior.

Gaia rotation/error variants, an independently defined HST rotation test, prior sensitivity and injection recovery follow. The report replay and mock-generator repairs are complete; use the source-run recipes in the modelling plan. Instrument scales remain a separate diagnostic, outside the compared sequence. New fits require an explicit request.

docs.title: Rung 1: all three models complete
docs.text:
Historical (2026-09)

Superseded by kb/models/jeans_comparison.md and kb/models/dm_fits.md.

The final cored-halo run completed successfully. Constant radial anisotropy improves the fit substantially in all three families. These are the next controlled baselines in the modelling ladder; the comparison remains conditional on spherical symmetry, constant anisotropy and the current rotation treatment.

Family Rung-0 χ² Rung-1 χ² Improvement Rung-1 ln Z K1: stars, remnants, central mass 771.53 342.51 429.02 20.36 ± 0.38 K2: NFW halo 763.12 316.01 447.11 30.53 ± 0.41 K2: cored halo 761.10 315.29 445.81 31.46 ± 0.35

All rows use the same 89 measurements; χ² is the total, not reduced χ². The three rung-1 likelihoods replay exactly from their saved inputs, with the same data fingerprint. The reconstructed legacy rung-0 likelihoods also replay and use the same data, although those older runs lack resolved input snapshots.

The cored run took 67 minutes and 820,972 likelihood calls. Its anisotropy is β = 0.1086 [0.1040, 0.1133] (median and 16–84% interval), consistent with the other families. Its conditional M_DM(<100 pc) posterior is 2.78 [1.79, 3.78] million solar masses, with a 95% upper limit of 4.34 million.

Cored versus NFW gives Δln Z = 0.93 ± 0.54, only a weak distinction. The halo families improve over K1 by Δln Z = 10.18 (NFW) and 11.11 (core) within this rung. The large improvement from rung 0 is driven mainly by the HST tangential profile; outer Gaia residuals still show that one constant β does not describe every radial regime. The natural next fit comparison is radial anisotropy variation and rotation, with the rung-0 and rung-1 results retained.

docs.title: Data with the two best-fitting models from each rung
docs.text:
PNG figure. NFW and cored are the two lowest-χ² families in each rung. Blue denotes NFW and orange denotes the core; dashed lines show rung 0 and solid lines show rung 1. Model markers are the actual likelihood predictions, including the measured-star/bin averages and streaming correction; lines connect those markers. Residuals use the same asymmetric errors as the likelihood, with the ±1σ interval shaded. The first MUSE bin starts at zero radius and its horizontal error bar is clipped by the log axis.

All four maximum likelihoods replay and their data fingerprints agree. The plotted numbers and provenance are saved in results/plot_data/. Regenerate it with PYTHONPATH=src python bin/plot_rung_data_comparison.py.

docs.title: Why the Gaia tangential fit worsens
docs.text:
Rung 1 optimises the joint likelihood. Its constant positive anisotropy improves HST strongly, while making the Gaia tangential predictions too low over several bins. For the cored model, the per-dataset changes are:

Dataset Rung-0 χ² Rung-1 χ² HST radial (21 bins) 152.44 69.66 HST tangential (21 bins) 483.75 88.59 MUSE LOS (29 bins) 75.96 51.25 Gaia radial (9 bins) 25.38 47.29 Gaia tangential (9 bins) 23.56 58.50

A controlled reevaluation isolates the anisotropy effect: keep every mass parameter and the distance at the rung-1 cored maximum-likelihood values, and change only β from 0.10698 to zero. Gaia tangential χ² falls to 14.93; HST radial and tangential χ² rise to 666.41 and 362.91. This is a diagnostic reevaluation, not a new fit. The corresponding NFW check changes Gaia tangential χ² from 62.23 to 17.78.

The cored rung-1 Gaia tangential residuals reach 3.32σ at 532 arcsec, 4.31σ at 662 arcsec and 3.56σ at 1328 arcsec. The last bin is 1.91σ low; it is not the main source of the deterioration. NFW and cored predictions are similar over this range, so this comparison principally identifies a limitation of constant anisotropy under the current tracer and rotation assumptions. Radially varying anisotropy, evaluated with consistent rotation controls, is the next comparison to test; its improvement must be measured by fitting.

The bin-level diagnostic records both saved fits and the fixed-mass β = 0 reevaluations.

docs.text:
Historical (2026-09)

Superseded by kb/models/jeans_comparison.md and kb/models/dm_fits.md.

Open the full-resolution PNG. Each column shows the best saved maximum-likelihood no-DM model and the lowest-χ² DM family at that stage. The cored halo wins the χ² selection over NFW in all four columns; this selection uses fit quality, not Bayesian evidence. Rung 2 is shown separately for the simple and flexible anisotropy profiles.

Stage No-DM χ² Selected DM χ² DM family Rung 0: isotropic 771.53 761.10 Cored Rung 1: constant β 342.51 315.29 Cored Rung 2: simple β(r) 263.83 259.19 Cored Rung 2: flexible β(r) 189.98 186.77 Cored

The five rows show HST radial and tangential proper motion, MUSE line-of-sight dispersion, and Gaia radial and tangential proper motion. docs.title: Numerical tests of Section 11 (tidally truncated DM around a heavy nucleus)
docs.text: 2026-09-21. Target: Section 11 of dm_capture_constraints.tex ("The equilibrium of tidally truncated dark matter around a heavy nucleus"). Code: src/ocen_dm/tails/truncated_equilibrium.py; tests tests/test_truncated_equilibrium.py.

docs.title: Status after the 2026-09-21 audit
docs.text:
Code update: DYNAMICAL_EXPERIMENTS.md describes the new initial-condition and live/frozen evolution drivers. The instantaneous tidal diagnostic has analytic circular-limit tests, and smoothly tapered joint equilibria have signed-DF and density-recovery checks. These provide machinery for the experiments below; the short software validation runs do not complete N2's hard energy-cut iteration or the long tidal experiments N3–N5.

N1 is the only completed experiment in the full grid specified below. The energy-cut formula is verified for its stated Kepler, isotropic, power-law assumptions; it is not a validated tidal-loss prescription. At 20 pc the class-3 shock estimate accumulates to 0.112 over 66 identical passages, not order unity. At 35 pc it reaches 1.52. Whether outer losses subsequently deplete the 20-pc density is a question for N3/N4. The previous N2 setup also counted the cluster's stellar mass twice; the revised component definitions below remove that ambiguity.

Completed pilot comparison (21 September 2026). Section 6 of the dynamical write-up now evaluates a fixed-potential energy cut in the actual cusp/core initial DFs and compares the scalar shock estimate with the completed 88-Myr live/frozen pilot. This supplies partial N2/N3/N5 evidence, without completing their proposed parameter grids or N2's self-consistent iteration. At 20 pc the instantaneous energy cut predicts 10.18%/14.71% density loss, while the live simulations give 2.50%/4.66%. The scalar pericentre energy estimate is much smaller than the full-orbit mean; extended internal orbits, disc crossings and continued work on escapers prevent interpreting that discrepancy as a fitted adiabatic correction. See results/plot_data/dynamical_analytics.json and bin/compare_dynamical_analytics.py.

docs.title: What Section 11 estimates, and what is actually uncertain
docs.text:
The section uses three approximations:

  1. Energy truncation. A tracer ρ ∝ r^−γ in the nucleus's Kepler potential has the isotropic DF f(E) ∝ (−E)^(γ−3/2); truncating it at Φ(r_J) leaves the fraction F_γ(x) = 1 − I_x(γ−½, 3/2) of the initial density at r = x r_J. At 20 pc: 0.35 (γ = 1, r_J = 70 pc), 0.14 (γ = 1, r_J = 35 pc), 0.60 / 0.28 for γ = 3/2.
  2. Re-adjustment is small, because a nucleus with total mass 3.55 × 10⁶ M☉ and approximate 3-D half-mass radius 7 pc can dominate low-DM models. Some grid choices have comparable DM mass; the small-response approximation must be checked model by model. The phase-mixing estimate is ~10⁸ yr.
  3. Shock heating per pericentre is ΔE/|E| ≈ (Δv/σ)² (1 + ω²τ²)^−γ_ad with γ_ad ≈ 1.5, giving much stronger local heating in class 3. The current arithmetic does not establish order-unity heating at 20 pc within that history.

Ranked by how much they can move the answer, the uncertainties are:

rank uncertainty size of the effect on ρ_DM(20 pc) 1 the definition of r_J — the simple r_peri[M/3M_host]^{1/3} gives 33 pc at the class-3 pericentre, a historical slope-corrected estimate was 59 pc, but has not been reproduced consistently ~3× (through F_γ(r/r_J)) 2 γ_ad and the impulsive approximation at ωτ ~ 1 factor ~2 in the number of passages to erosion 3 departures from Kepler (Plummer core inside ~10 pc, stars, DM self-gravity near r_J) tens of per cent 4 anisotropy of the initial cusp (radial loses more, tangential less) tens of per cent 5 the closed-form algebra itself none — verified, see N1

The experiments below are ordered by cost. N1 is done; N0 + N2 + N3 is one working day and covers ranks 1–3; N4 produces the number the white-dwarf comparison needs.

docs.title: N1 — the truncation formula (DONE, minutes)
docs.text:
Set-up. Two independent checks with G = M = r_J = 1. (a) Direct quadrature of the physical Eddington integral ρ_t(r)/ρ(r) = ∫{Φ(r)}^{Φ(r_J)} (−E)^(γ−3/2) √(E−Φ(r)) dE ÷ ∫ (…) dE, without the substitution that produces the beta function. (b) Monte Carlo: sample p(v) ∝ v² (−E)^(γ−3/2) at fixed r by numerical inverse-CDF, cut E > Φ(r_J), measure the surviving fraction. Uses no beta-function identity.}^{0

Result — passed in the recorded N1 experiment. Quadrature agrees with 1 − I_x(γ−½, 3/2) to 2 × 10⁻¹⁶ (γ = 1) and 6 × 10⁻¹⁷ (γ = 3/2) at x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.6. Monte Carlo with 4 × 10⁵ samples agrees within 1.1 σ at all six points. The committed unit test (test_truncation_formula_against_monte_carlo) uses 4 × 10⁴ samples per case and a four-sigma tolerance; it is a smaller regression check than the recorded 4 × 10⁵-sample experiment. The sampler is local to the test, not yet a reusable phase-space initial-condition generator.

Two sampler bugs found on the way, both of which would have propagated into N2–N4 because they reuse this machinery: * a rejection-sampling envelope that is not an upper bound when γ < 3/2 (the weight v²(−E)^(γ−3/2) diverges as v → v_esc): it under-sampled exactly the loosely bound particles that truncation removes, and inflated the retained fraction from 0.60 to 0.87 — a 24 σ error that looked like a failure of the formula; * trapezoidal CDF bias at the integrable endpoint singularity (0.6 %, 5 σ at 2 × 10⁵ samples), removed by sampling in θ with v = v_esc sin θ.

docs.title: N0 — what is r_J, really? (minutes, no dynamics)
docs.text:
Set-up. First recover the circular, spherical reference r_J³ = G M_sat / (Omega² - d²Phi/dR²), with Omega² = G M_host(<R)/R³. Thus the enclosed-mass denominator is 3 − d ln M_host/d ln R, not 2 minus that slope. For a point-mass host the coefficient is 3; for a flat circular-speed curve it is 2. This follows by differentiating dPhi/dR = GM_host/R²; see the galpy tidal-radius definition.

Then evaluate the tidal tensor T_ij = -d²Phi/dx_i dx_j along each orbit, add the instantaneous centrifugal matrix for an explicitly defined rotating frame, and solve lambda_max r³ = G M_sat(<r) where a disruptive eigenvalue is positive. Compare with the existing coefficient-3 proxy and the circular spherical reference. An eccentric orbit in a slowing bar has no conserved Jacobi integral: this is an instantaneous scale, not an exact escape surface. Record the angular velocity and treatment of time-dependent terms. Report the value at pericentre and its variation around the orbit; do it in McMillan 2017, Hunter et al. 2024 axisymmetrised, and the barred Hunter potential at Ω_b = 24 (where the non-axisymmetric term contributes directly).

Verifies. Rank-1 uncertainty. It is the input to every F_γ number in the section, and the historical estimates differ by 1.8× (33 vs 59 pc), enough to change the retention factor substantially. Recalculate both under explicit conventions rather than treating the unverified 59-pc estimate as a validated reference.

Validation. Recover the point-mass and flat-rotation circular limits and converge the force derivatives. Report the convention spread as a systematic. A barred/axisymmetric difference above 20% is a physical result to investigate, not a numerical test failure.

Cost. Minutes. No new machinery beyond forceDeriv.

docs.title: N2 — truncated equilibrium in the true potential (minutes, AGAMA, no dynamics)
docs.text:
Set-up. Define the baryonic mass once. Use either (a) a rigid Plummer approximation with total nucleus mass 3.55 × 10⁶ M☉ and a = 5.4 pc for a 7-pc 3-D half-mass radius, or (b) the full K1 stellar MGE + remnant + point-mass model, reconstructed from one saved parameter vector and its distance. Do not add a 2.9 × 10⁶ M☉ cluster MGE on top of a 3.55 × 10⁶ M☉ Plummer representing that same cluster. An extra dwarf stellar envelope, if included, needs its own mass and profile.

Add the DM model (NFW 10⁹/10¹⁰/10¹¹ M☉ with stated z = 2 concentrations, plus contracted and cored variants). Compute the DM DF in the combined potential, apply the energy cut at Phi(r_J), and iterate the DM potential to a stated convergence tolerance. Check recovered density and moments before and after sampling. AGAMA clips negative DF values, so a successful QuasiSpherical construction is not a positivity test. The gamma = 0 variant cannot use the gamma > 1/2 Kepler power-law formula.

Measure M_DM(<r)/M_baryon(<r) throughout the domain. If DM is not subdominant, bring self-gravity into the experiment at this stage; do not assume all grid points qualify for N3/N4's test-particle treatment and postpone the check until N5.

Variants. (a) apocentre criterion r_apo(E, L) > r_J instead of the energy cut — these differ because a high-L orbit with E above Φ(r_J) never reaches r_J; the two bracket the truth. (b) radially and tangentially anisotropic initial DFs (β = ±0.3), which is rank-4.

Verifies. Rank 3 and 4: how much the Plummer core (inside ~10 pc), the stellar mass and the DM self-gravity break the Kepler idealisation behind F_γ.

Pass criterion / deliverable. ρ_t(r)/ρ(r) at 3, 10, 20 pc tabulated against F_γ; the difference quoted as the "non-Kepler correction". This output replaces the e^{−r/r_J} stand-in in the density figure of Section 9 — the one number in the note that is currently a placeholder.

Cost. Minutes per model, ~1 h for the whole grid.

docs.title: N3 — one pericentre passage, test particles (≈ 1 h)
docs.text:
Set-up. 10⁵ massless particles sampled from the N2 equilibrium, orbiting an analytic nucleus whose centre follows the precomputed class-1 (r_peri = 1.57 kpc, v_peri = 387 km/s) or class-3 (0.42 kpc, 507 km/s) orbit; integrate with agama.orbit in the inertial frame, the potential being host + Plummer nucleus with a time-dependent center read from the orbit track. Run from apocentre to apocentre across one pericentre. Measure ΔE in the nucleus frame per particle, binned by initial radius (10, 20, 35, 50, 70 pc).

Verifies. Rank 2 — the entire shock table of Section 11, including the adiabatic correction, and it fits γ_ad instead of assuming 1.5. No self-gravity, no softening, no relaxation, so the result is clean.

Pass criterion. The impulsive scaling ΔE ∝ r² recovered where ωτ ≪ 1; the measured suppression at ωτ ≳ 1 within a factor 2 of (1 + ω²τ²)^−γ_ad; γ_ad fitted to ±0.3. A measured ΔE/|E| more than 3× the analytic value at 20 pc would reject the amplitude of that local approximation in a matched shock experiment. It would not by itself establish destruction of the 20-pc density. The completed pilot shows why: a small fraction of extended or escaping internal orbits can dominate the full-orbit cohort mean while most inner density remains. Isolated-shock calibration must match the forcing history, internal orbital frequencies, statistic and energy normalization before applying this criterion.

Cost. ~1 h including set-up. This is the highest value-per-hour experiment in the list.

docs.title: N4 — many passages: the number the WD comparison needs (hours)
docs.text:
Updated scope (21 September 2026). The long-term evolution plan specifies the density histories, stellar-survival comparisons and convergence controls now required. The frozen, rigid-nucleus experiments below establish conditional DM evolution. A present-day survival constraint additionally requires a responsive nucleus. The implemented class-3 history spans 8 natural units = 7.82234 Gyr; its original clock must be preserved. The costs below are planning estimates, not measured production runtimes.

Set-up. As N3 but integrating the full histories: the class-1 orbit for 10 Gyr (~114 pericentres) and the class-3 debris orbit for 8 Gyr (~66), the latter also once in the time-dependent barred potential of the companion note. Track the bound mass (energy in the nucleus frame < 0) and ρ_DM at 3, 10, 20, 35, 50, 70 pc as functions of time, with output every ~50 Myr and densely around pericentre.

Tests. The combination of truncation and shocks: whether the density at 20 pc is truncation-limited (classes 1–2 — the prediction is that it settles at F_γ × the initial cusp and then stays put) or continues to decline as outer orbits are heated (a class-3 hypothesis). The local 20-pc heating estimate alone does not predict rapid erosion there.

Scientific comparison. Test whether the final class-1/2 density lies within a factor 2 of F_γ × ρ_initial, and measure rather than require a class-3 decline. Disagreement can falsify the approximation. Numerical validation: converge with two particle numbers (10⁴, 10⁵) and two time steps; separate numerical error from the physical discrepancy.

Deliverable. The corrected ρ_DM(20 pc) per orbital class, which is what enters the white-dwarf heating comparison and the local DM mass fraction f_DM.

Cost. Hours (test particles in an analytic potential; no tree gravity).

docs.title: N5 — is the test-particle approximation valid? (one run)
docs.text:
Set-up. Repeat one N4 case with a live DM component (10⁵ particles, pyfalcon or gyrfalcON, softening ≤ 1 pc) around the rigid nucleus potential.

Verifies. That neglecting DM self-gravity is safe — checked first from N2's enclosed-mass ratios. Some initial profiles exceed 10⁶ M☉ inside 70 pc, so this approximation is not valid across the grid by assumption.

Pass criterion. Bound mass and ρ(20 pc) within 20 % of the test-particle run. If it passes, N3–N4 can be used for the full grid of halo masses and concentrations at negligible cost.

docs.title: N6 — stellar two-body heating (estimate only, no simulation)
docs.text: Diffusion coefficients from the Spitzer formulae with the K1 stellar density and remnant population, integrated over 10 Gyr, to check that the DM inside ~5 pc is not heated out by the stars. An N-body treatment is out of scope; the estimate decides whether it needs to be in scope.

docs.title: Summary of the programme
docs.text:
what it settles cost status N1 the closed-form truncation factor minutes done, passed N0 the definition of r_J (largest single uncertainty) minutes to do N2 non-Kepler corrections; replaces the e^{−r/r_J} model in the figure ~1 h to do N3 the shock table; calibrates γ_ad ~1 h to do N4 ρ_DM(20 pc) per orbital class — the number the WD comparison needs hours to do N5 validity of test particles one run to do N6 stellar heating inside 5 pc estimate to do

Minimum useful set: N0 + N2 + N3 (one working day), which fixes the r_J convention, replaces the placeholder density model with a computed one, and calibrates the shock formula. N4 then produces the final numbers.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The working environment is a Python virtual environment with AGAMA, JamPy (non-commercial licence, imported, never vendored), UltraNest and the usual scientific stack. From the repository root:

source <venv>/bin/activate
export PYTHONPATH=src
python -m ocen_dm.cli --help        # or the installed entry point `ocen`
python -m ocen_dm.cli inventory     # what data are present

ocen is declared in pyproject.toml; ocen-dm is not a command.

docs.title: External locations
docs.text:
Inputs that are not in the repository are found through environment variables; nothing in the code assumes a machine-specific path.

Variable Contents Needed by OCEN_CATALOGUES shared catalogue store: Vasiliev & Baumgardt 2021 members and cluster zip, Baumgardt GC tables, STREAMFINDER, HST Large Programme, Tango archive provenance checks, Gaia products, all stream scripts OCEN_ISOCHRONES MIST grids prepared with minimint (minimint_hst/ with the HST filters) mass function, HST CMD plots OCEN_BAR_DIR clone of oCen_bar (Hunter+2024 and Portail+2017 potentials, GSE contours) barred hosts, bar migration, stream fits NEMO_DIR NEMO/falcON build bin/nemo_env.sh (gyrfalcON runs) PYTHON interpreter for the shell drivers (default python) bin/*.sh

Put them in a file named .env in the repository root. It is gitignored, so the locations never enter the repository, and import ocen_dm reads it, so scripts, tests and fits find the inputs without any shell setup (bin/nemo_env.sh reads NEMO_DIR from it too):

# .env -- one NAME=value per line; ~ and $VAR are expanded
OCEN_CATALOGUES=/path/to/catalogues
OCEN_ISOCHRONES=/path/to/isochrones
OCEN_BAR_DIR=/path/to/oCen_bar
NEMO_DIR=/path/to/nemo

A variable exported in the shell always wins over the file. An unset variable shows up literally in the error message, for example FileNotFoundError: ... '$OCEN_CATALOGUES/streamfinder_ibata2024_dr3.fits'.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
python -m ocen_dm.cli fetch-data    # registered downloads, checksums verified
python -m ocen_dm.cli preprocess    # standardised catalogues and published profiles
python -m ocen_dm.cli plot-data
  • One journal supplement (Kuzma et al. 2026) needs manual retrieval; Fimbulthul is now fetched from VizieR.
  • data/raw/omegacat_vi_kinematics may be a local link to an external copy of the oMEGACat VI data rather than a directory in the checkout.
  • Our own HST and Gaia PM profiles and the count products have separate builders (kinematics/hst_profile.py, kinematics/outer_gaia.py, bin/build_count_profiles.py). Loaders build missing products automatically, so a fresh checkout can write data on first use.
  • External catalogues live in a shared store ($OCEN_CATALOGUES) and are referenced, not copied; some model inputs come from a clone of oCen_bar. See Data products.

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text:
• Fits are launched only when requested, with a fresh output label; a run directory is never reused. Every batch freezes its source, configuration and inputs (with sha256), so it can be replayed exactly.
  • The base model is fitted with bin/run_compact_df_recovery.py; the exact command is on the base model page.
  • The older Jeans fits use python -m ocen_dm.cli fit with explicit switches (see the modelling plan); a bare fit selects an outdated default.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
python -m pytest tests -q

The full suite includes local-data and optional-engine tests and takes about 13-25 min; some tests skip without those inputs. pytest-xdist (in the dev extra of pyproject.toml) runs it in parallel:

python -m pytest tests -q -n 6

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Units: internal dynamics in pc, M☉ and km/s; Galactic-orbit modules carry their own explicit conversions (AGAMA time unit = 977.8 Myr).
  • Plots are PNG files in plots/; plotted tables and JSON provenance go to results/plot_data/. Compiled PDFs sit next to their LaTeX in docs/.
  • data/ and results/ are not committed.
  • Results are recorded in a project journal that is kept locally (not in git); the reports in docs/ carry the results that are shared.
  • External reviews go to docs/reviews/.

docs.title: Building this site
docs.text:
source <venv>/bin/activate
mkdocs serve            # local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict   # the link check used before publishing
mkdocs gh-deploy        # publish to GitHub Pages

The build hook (docs/hooks/kb.py) serves plots/, generates the registered sources and literature pages from committed files, and points code links to GitHub.

docs.title: Simulation outputs
docs.text: Spray, N-body and dynamics outputs are large (about 14 GB) and live outside the repository, in $OCEN_SIMS (set in .env). results/streams, results/nbody and results/dynamics are local links to $OCEN_SIMS/streams, /nbody and /dynamics, so the scripts' repository-relative paths still work. On a new machine, create the three links after copying the data.

docs.title: Comparison with published mass models
docs.text:
How our two no-DM models (the DF base model and the Jeans comparison model) compare with published models of Omega Centauri's mass distribution. Published numbers are taken from the papers' abstracts (checked in ADS, 2026-10-14) unless marked otherwise; all papers are in the SciX library.

Summary

  • Total mass and M/L agree within the spread of published values. Our total M/L_V of 2.8 is close to Watkins+2013 (2.71); our total mass, 3.27×10⁶ M☉ (DF best fit, M★ + M_rem), is 13–22% below the recent estimates of 3.7–4.2×10⁶ M☉ (D'Souza & Rix 2013 scaled to our distance; the Baumgardt database).
  • The central dark mass is where the literature splits, and our two models fall on the two sides. The Jeans model's black hole (posterior median 4.25×10⁴ M☉; 3.67×10⁴ M☉ with the star-count tracer, J-counts) reproduces the classic IMBH claims (Noyola+2008/2010, Baumgardt 2017, Jalali+2012). The DF model's compact remnant component (2.7×10⁵ M☉, 2.2 pc scale, 8% of the mass, no black hole) matches the "extended central mass" picture: 2–3×10⁵ M☉ favoured by kinematics plus pulsar timing (Bañares-Hernández+2025: 2.65×10⁵ M☉ in a Plummer of 1.88 pc, the same form, mass and nearly the same scale as ours) and ~5% of the mass in stellar-mass black holes (Zocchi+2019, Baumgardt+2019, Dickson+2024). The remnant mass is weakly constrained: the tied, completeness-corrected DF refit gives 2.00×10⁵ M☉ (1.88 pc) with predictions that differ by a few per cent, and J-counts puts 8.4×10⁵ M☉ in remnants (posterior median).
  • Anisotropy: the DF profile (isotropic core, mildly radial at intermediate radii, tangential outside) agrees with oMEGACat VI and van de Ven+2006; the Jeans model's tangential core does not.
  • The fast-moving stars require a point mass of at least 8,200 M☉ (Häberle+2024, robust bound). Their model-dependent estimates go higher (≥ 21,100 M☉ with accelerations; 39,000–47,000 M☉ preferred by an N-body comparison, which brackets our Jeans black hole). With a fixed point mass the DF still fits (DF + central black hole): 8,200 M☉ lowers the objective by 5.5; 4×10⁴ M☉ fits the central kinematics better (χ²_kin −12) but over-predicts the central HST counts (+15), so the objective falls by only 1.0. Neither difference is calibrated.

docs.title: Total mass, mass-to-light ratio and distance
docs.text:
Proper-motion-based masses scale as \(M\propto D^3\) and M/L as \(\propto D\); published values are given at their own distance, and scaled to ours (5.356 kpc) only where the paper states the scaling.

Study Method D [kpc] Total mass [10⁶ M☉] M/L_V This work, DF base model spherical action DF, HST+MUSE+Gaia kinematics, star counts 5.356 (prior 5.43 ± 0.05) 3.27 (best fit; tied refit 3.28) 2.8 (stellar 2.6) This work, Jeans model (J-Trager) spherical Jeans, black hole, same kinematics 5.34 (ML), 5.36 (median) 3.18 (ML), 3.24 (median) 2.7 (ML), 2.8 (median) (stellar 2.0, 2.3) van de Ven+2006 axisymmetric Schwarzschild, ground-based PMs + LOS 4.8 ± 0.3 (fitted) 2.5 ± 0.3 2.5 ± 0.1 Watkins+2013 discrete axisymmetric Jeans 4.59 ± 0.08 (fitted) — 2.71 ± 0.05 D'Souza & Rix 2013 discrete PM likelihood scaled to 5.356 4.20 (spherical isotropic), 3.74 (flattened) — Baumgardt GC database N-body grid (catalogue value; version unrecorded, UNVERIFIED against the live database) 5.43 3.94 — Merritt+1997 non-parametric, 469 LOS velocities — — mass "slightly more extended than" the light

D'Souza & Rix give \(4.55\times10^6\,(D/5.5\,{\rm kpc})^3\) M☉ (spherical) and \(4.05\times10^6\,(D/5.5\,{\rm kpc})^3\) M☉ (flattened); at 5.356 kpc the factor is 0.923.

  • M/L is close to published values: our total M/L_V of 2.8 is slightly above Watkins (2.71) and van de Ven (2.5). Scaled to our distance with M/L ∝ D their values would be 3.2 and 2.8; their distances were fitted jointly, so this scaling is only indicative. Our total masses are M★ + M_rem (+ M_BH for Jeans).

  • Our total mass is 13–22% below the recent estimates at our distance (3.27 against 3.74–4.20×10⁶ M☉ from D'Souza & Rix and 3.94×10⁶ M☉ from the Baumgardt database). van de Ven+2006 found 2.5×10⁶ M☉ at 4.8 kpc. Possible reasons, not yet tested: our model is spherical (D'Souza & Rix find flattening lowers the mass by 10%, in the same direction, so it does not explain it); our kinematics reach ~60 pc and the mass beyond is extrapolated; the Gaia data may have systematics in the outer bins; and the Baumgardt value comes from mass-segregated N-body models.

  • Distance: ours (5.356 kpc) is pulled by the prior; the oMEGACat VI kinematic distance is 5.494 ± 0.061 kpc (Häberle+2025), 2.2σ larger. At 5.494 kpc our proper-motion masses would be ~8% higher.

docs.title: The central dark mass
docs.text:
Study Method Central dark mass This work, Jeans model spherical Jeans, β₀ ≤ −½ imposed IMBH 4.25×10⁴ M☉ (posterior median; 95% interval 3.6–4.9×10⁴); 3.67 (3.30–4.02)×10⁴ M☉ with the star-count tracer (J-counts; median, 16–84%) This work, DF base model self-consistent DF, isotropic core no IMBH; remnants 2.7×10⁵ M☉ in a 2.2 pc Plummer (8% of the mass) (best fit; tied refit 2.00×10⁵ M☉, 1.88 pc). Fixed point masses of 8,200 and 4×10⁴ M☉ are compatible with the fit (DF + central black hole) Noyola+2008 isotropic spherical, Gemini + HST IMBH 4.0 (+0.75/−1.0) ×10⁴ M☉ Noyola+2010 VLT kinematics IMBH (4.7 ± 1.0) ×10⁴ M☉ Jalali+2012 N-body, isotropic multimass King ICs IMBH 5×10⁴ M☉ (2% of the stellar mass) Baumgardt 2017 N-body grid IMBH ~4×10⁴ M☉ van der Marel & Anderson 2010 anisotropic spherical Jeans, HST PMs core models fit with M_BH = 0; M_BH ≲ 1.2×10⁴ (1σ), ≲ 1.8×10⁴ M☉ (3σ) Zocchi+2017 radially anisotropic limepy central kinematics fitted without an IMBH Zocchi+2019 multimass limepy ~5% of the mass in stellar-mass black holes Baumgardt+2019 N-body grid + fast-star test no IMBH; 4.6% of the mass in a central cluster of stellar-mass black holes Evans+2022 axisymmetric Jeans, dark + luminous components non-luminous component ≲ 10⁶ M☉ within r_h preferred over constant M/L; a compact remnant core can supply up to ~5×10⁵ M☉ Dickson+2024 multimass models black-hole mass fraction above 5% Häberle+2024 seven fast-moving stars in the central 3″ (0.08 pc), multi-epoch HST; projected velocities 66–113 km/s against a no-IMBH escape velocity of 62 km/s IMBH ≥ 8,200 M☉ (robust bound: velocities and escape velocity only). Model-dependent: ≥ 21,100 M☉ (99%) with the measured accelerations (all consistent with zero within 3σ); an N-body comparison of the inner 10″ prefers 39,000–47,000 M☉ and disfavours no IMBH, a stellar-mass black-hole cluster and > 50,000 M☉, with the authors' caveat of low number statistics (full text, main text p. 3) Bañares-Hernández+2025 Jeans (GravSphere) + millisecond-pulsar accelerations extended central mass ~2–3×10⁵ M☉ favoured over an IMBH; IMBH < 6×10³ M☉ (3σ)
  • Our two models reproduce the two sides of the debate with the same data. The black-hole mass of our Jeans model is the classic value (4–5×10⁴ M☉). That value comes from models with isotropic or imposed central anisotropy; in ours the black hole is tied to β₀ at its −½ bound and gains Δχ² ≈ 6 from a few bins inside 0.3 pc.
  • The DF model's dark mass is the "extended central mass". Its remnant component, 2.7×10⁵ M☉ with a 2.2 pc scale (half-mass radius 2.8 pc), matches the 2–3×10⁵ M☉ that Bañares-Hernández+2025 favour from kinematics and pulsar timing, the ~5% stellar-mass black-hole fraction of Zocchi+2019, Baumgardt+2019 and Dickson+2024, and the ≲ 5×10⁵ M☉ remnant core that Evans+2022 allow. Our component is a generic Plummer, so it can also contain white dwarfs and neutron stars.
  • The fast-moving stars set a robust lower bound on a point mass. Häberle+2024 find ≥ 8,200 M☉ from the velocities and escape velocity alone. This already exceeds the 3σ upper limit of Bañares-Hernández+2025 (6×10³ M☉): the published results are in tension. Their model-dependent estimates are higher: ≥ 21,100 M☉ (99%) when the accelerations (all within 3σ of zero) are modelled, and 39,000–47,000 M☉ preferred by a comparison with N-body models of the inner 10″, which also disfavours a stellar-mass black-hole cluster without an IMBH; the authors caution that low number statistics limit that comparison. The 21,100 M☉ limit would also exceed the 3σ limit of van der Marel & Anderson 2010 (1.8×10⁴ M☉).
  • Our two models map onto that tension. The Jeans black hole (posterior median 4.25×10⁴ M☉; 3.67×10⁴ M☉ for J-counts) lies inside or near Häberle's preferred range; the DF model's extended remnants match Bañares-Hernández. The DF fitted with a fixed point mass (DF + central black hole, 2026-10-15) gives objective 275.2 at 8,200 M☉ and 279.7 at 4×10⁴ M☉, against 280.7 without; the 4×10⁴ M☉ cusp over-predicts the central HST counts. These fits use the 2026-10-13 count likelihood and are not calibrated with mocks.

docs.title: Remnant mass and spatial scale
docs.text:
Numbers from the full texts (arXiv versions, read 2026-10-14), with their location in each paper. Values marked computed are ours, derived from the paper's numbers as shown.

Study Component (definition) Mass [M☉] Fraction Form and scale Total mass, distance Where This work, DF base model (best fit) remnant Plummer: all mass not following the counted light 2.73×10⁵ 8.4% Plummer, a = 2.18 pc (3D; half-mass 2.85 pc) 3.27×10⁶, 5.356 kpc base model This work, tied DF refit (best fit) as above, completeness-corrected counts, tied amplitude ratio 2.00×10⁵ 6.1% Plummer, a = 1.88 pc (3D; half-mass 2.5 pc) 3.28×10⁶, 5.359 kpc tied refit This work, Jeans model (J-Trager) (posterior median) remnant Plummer + black hole 5.4×10⁵ + 4.25×10⁴ 16.5% + 1.3% Plummer, a = 5.3 pc (3D) 3.24×10⁶, 5.36 kpc Jeans model This work, J-counts (posterior median) remnant Plummer + black hole 8.4×10⁵ + 3.67×10⁴ 26.7% + 1.2% Plummer, a = 5.1 pc (3D) 3.16×10⁶, 5.36 kpc J-counts Bañares-Hernández+2025 "extended central mass" on top of a light-traced M★ (which includes remnants that follow the light); interpreted as stellar-mass black holes 2.65 ± 0.19×10⁵; 2.20×10⁵ without the pulsar accelerations; 2.1–3.1×10⁵ across centres and profile shapes 9.0% (computed: 2.65/(26.8+2.65)) Plummer, r_cen = 1.88 ± 0.10 pc (3D; 1.59 pc without pulsars); Gaussian alternative σ = 1.37 pc M★ = 2.68 ± 0.05×10⁶; 5.2 kpc fixed Fig. 2, Table 2, Secs. 6, 8–9, App. B–D Baumgardt+2019 stellar-mass black holes only 1.65×10⁵ 4.6 ± 0.5% mass-segregated N-body; radius not given ("centrally concentrated") 5.24 kpc adopted Secs. 4–5 Zocchi+2019 black holes as the dark component of two-component limepy models (white dwarfs and neutron stars in the visible component) 1.35×10⁵ (computed: F₂ × M) 4.5 (+4.0/−2.5)% anisotropic; 5.2% isotropic not fully segregated, extending to about the half-mass radius (r_h = 8.57 pc); ~1.4×10³ M☉ within 0.2 pc 3.01×10⁶, 5.14 kpc (fitted) Table 2, Secs. 3–4 Dickson+2024 (i) black holes; (ii) all dark remnants (white dwarfs, neutron stars, black holes) (i) 1.82×10⁵ (12,400 black holes, mean 14.8 M☉) (i) 5.9 ± 0.2% (statistical only); (ii) 50.3% multimass limepy; radius not given ("concentrated within the central regions") in their Paper I Table 1, Sec. 5.3 Evans+2022 generic non-luminous component (remnants or dark matter) 10⁴–10⁶ within the ~6 pc half-light radius (posterior contours only) — NFW with r_max ≲ 1 pc (r_s = r_max/2.16), or Gaussian 5.24 kpc fixed Secs. 6–7, Figs. 5, 7

Like-for-like with the closest model (Bañares-Hernández+2025, same Plummer form):

DF base model (best fit) Bañares-Hernández+2025 Mass 2.73×10⁵ M☉ (tied refit 2.00×10⁵) 2.65 ± 0.19×10⁵ M☉ Plummer scale 2.18 pc (tied refit 1.88) 1.88 ± 0.10 pc at 5.2 kpc; 1.94 pc scaled to 5.356 kpc (computed) Mass fraction 8.4% 9.0% M(<1 pc), M(<3 pc) (computed) 2.0×10⁴, 1.45×10⁵ M☉ 2.7×10⁴, 1.61×10⁵ M☉ Data HST, MUSE, Gaia kinematics; star counts stellar kinematics, surface density, millisecond-pulsar positions and accelerations Method self-consistent action DF Jeans (GravSphere)
  • The DF remnant component reproduces the Bañares-Hernández central mass: the same mass within 3%, a scale 12% larger once both are at the same distance, and the same mass fraction. They reach it with a different method and with pulsar timing; from stellar kinematics alone they find a smaller and more compact component (2.20×10⁵ M☉, 1.59 pc).
  • The black-hole-only estimates are lower, 1.35–1.82×10⁵ M☉ (4.5–5.9%). That is expected: our component also holds whatever neutron stars and segregated white dwarfs do not follow the light, whereas those models put white dwarfs and neutron stars in the visible or light-traced mass (in Dickson+2024 all dark remnants make up 50% of the mass).
  • Scales: besides Bañares-Hernández, only Evans+2022 constrain one (r_max ≲ 1 pc for an NFW), and Zocchi+2019 give a qualitative extent (to about the half-mass radius, 8.6 pc). The concentration differs between models: within 0.2 pc Zocchi's black-hole component holds ~1.4×10³ M☉, against ~300 M☉ for the Bañares-Hernández Plummer and ~200 M☉ for ours (computed for the Plummer models).
  • The Jeans model's remnant component (5.4×10⁵ M☉ at 5.3 pc) is twice as massive and 2.5 times more extended than any of these; its central mass is carried by the black hole instead.
  • The agreement depends on the fit. The tied, completeness-corrected refit gives 2.00×10⁵ M☉ in a 1.88 pc Plummer: 25% below the Bañares-Hernández mass, with a scale 3% below theirs at our distance (1.94 pc), while its predictions differ from the base fit by a few per cent.
  • Our remnant mass is the least constrained of our numbers. It trades against the stellar mass (±23% on mocks), pinning the mass per counted star between 8 and 12 M☉ moves it from 1.6 to 4.4×10⁵ M☉, the tied refit moves it by −27%, and J-counts puts 8.4×10⁵ M☉ in remnants.

How these remnant masses relate to the stellar mass and the IMF, and which are physically allowed: Remnant mass and the stellar population.

Caveat: the Bañares-Hernández values are from arXiv:2408.00939v6, which may differ in detail from the journal version; in it, the Sec. 8.1 statement on the centre dependence does not match the Fig. C.1 numbers.

docs.title: Anisotropy
docs.text:
Study Anisotropy This work, DF base model isotropic core; radial, peak β ≈ +0.15 near 8 pc; tangential beyond ~22 pc (−0.53 at 100 pc) This work, Jeans model tangential core (β₀ ≈ −0.52, imposed ≤ −½); radial +0.15 at 3–15 pc; tangential outside Häberle+2025 (oMEGACat VI) isotropic in the core, increasing radial anisotropy outwards (HST field) Watkins+2013 mildly radial, β = 0.10 ± 0.02 (single value) van de Ven+2006 close to isotropic inside ~10′, increasingly tangential outside Zocchi+2017 radially anisotropic models fit the central kinematics
  • The DF profile matches the published picture: isotropic core, radially biased within the HST field, tangential in the outskirts. Our zero crossing (~22 pc, 14′ at our distance) is near van de Ven's ~10′ transition.
  • The Jeans model's tangential core disagrees with the isotropic core measured directly by oMEGACat VI. It is a consequence of the black hole (a cored tracer around a point mass needs β₀ ≤ −½), which is a further argument against taking its black-hole mass at face value.

docs.title: Dark matter
docs.text: Evans+2022 find a non-luminous component of ≲ 10⁶ M☉ within the half-light radius strongly preferred over a constant-M/L stellar model and leave open that part of it is dark matter. Our models agree that a centrally concentrated non-luminous mass is needed (2.7×10⁵ M☉ in the DF model, ~6×10⁵ M☉ of remnants plus black hole in the Jeans model), but find that it can be supplied by remnants without dark matter. Our dark-matter variants show that the data constrain the total mass profile, not how it splits between stars, remnants and dark matter (Results).

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No comparison yet with published axisymmetric or rotating models on our data; ours are spherical.
  • The published total masses use different data and extents; a like-for-like test (our pipeline on their data, or theirs on ours) has not been done.
  • Earlier literature numbers assembled for the Jeans fits: Literature baselines.

docs.title: Remnant mass and the stellar population
docs.text:
How much mass can be in stellar remnants (white dwarfs, neutron stars, stellar-mass black holes), how it is tied to the stellar mass through the initial mass function (IMF), and whether the remnant components of our two models are physically sensible.

Summary

  • The remnant mass is tied to the stellar mass through the IMF, the initial–final mass relation, natal-kick retention and the cluster's escape history. For a Kroupa IMF at 12.5 Gyr, remnants are 25–31% of the present mass (white dwarfs 23–25%, black holes 0–8%, neutron stars < 1%); dynamical loss of low-mass stars raises this to ~50% in published fits of omega Cen.
  • Our "remnant" component is not the total remnant mass. Most white dwarfs (mean 0.59 M☉) are lighter than the ~0.8 M☉ stars that trace the light, are no more concentrated than them, and sit in the light-following stellar mass. The extra Plummer component can only represent mass more concentrated than the tracers: black holes, neutron stars and white dwarfs heavier than 0.8 M☉.
  • That budget is 8.7–11.8% of the total mass for a Kroupa IMF with all black holes retained, against published omega Cen black-hole fractions of 4.5–6% (up to ~8% in 2026 preprints).
  • The DF model passes (best fit 8.4% of the total, M_rem/M★ = 0.09; tied, completeness-corrected refit 6.1%, 0.065); the Jeans model does not (18–26% including its black hole, M_rem/M★ ≈ 0.2; 28–32% with the star-count tracer, J-counts): its component is too massive to be remnants and more plausibly absorbs a radial M/L variation.
  • M_rem is weakly constrained. The tied refit lowers it from 2.73 to 2.00×10⁵ M☉ with predictions that change by a few per cent; J-counts puts 8.4×10⁵ M☉ (posterior median) in remnants.
  • Proposed priors (not adopted; a model change needs a decision): M_rem/M★ ~ HalfNormal(0.10) truncated at 0.30, and a remnant scale below the stellar half-mass radius.

docs.title: The bookkeeping
docs.text:
The cluster mass is living stars plus remnants, \(M_{\rm cl}=M_{\rm live}+M_R\), with \(M_R=M_{\rm WD}+M_{\rm NS}+M_{\rm BH}\). Our models decompose it differently:

\[ \rho_{\rm tot}(r)=M_\star\,\hat\rho_L(r)+M_{\rm rem}\,\hat\rho_P(r)\;[+M_\bullet\,\delta(\mathbf r)], \]

where \(\hat\rho_L\) follows the counted light and \(\hat\rho_P\) is a Plummer sphere. \(M_\star\) contains every remnant that is distributed like the light; \(M_{\rm rem}\) is the mass the light-following profile cannot accommodate. Hence \(M_{\rm rem}\neq M_R\): a prior on all remnants applied to \(M_{\rm rem}\) would double-count. Bañares-Hernández+2025 make the same distinction (their photometric mass includes remnants traced by the light).

Both are tied to the IMF through a shared normalisation,

\[ M_i=A\int\xi(m)\,m_{i,\rm final}(m,Z)\,P_{i,\rm bound}(m,t)\,dm, \qquad M_{\rm live}=A\int_{m<m_{\rm TO}}\xi(m)\,m\,P_{\rm bound}(m,t)\,dm, \]

so the remnant mass cannot be chosen independently of the stars unless the formation and escape history is also allowed to change.

docs.title: The IMF budget
docs.text:
Assumptions: Kroupa IMF (0.08–100 M☉), turnoff 0.79 M☉ (our MIST fit), white dwarfs from 0.79–8 M☉ with \(m_{\rm WD}=0.109\,m_i+0.394\) (Kalirai+2008), neutron stars of 1.3 M☉ from 8–20 M☉, black holes from > 20 M☉ with \(m_{\rm BH}=f\,m_i\) capped at 40 M☉ (f = 0.25 or 0.4 for low metallicity), and no escape of stars. Script: bin/remnant_budget.py.

Retention (NS, BH) m_BH = f m_i Stars White dwarfs Neutron stars Black holes All remnants Heavier than the tracers 10%, 0% — 75.2% 24.6% 0.2% 0% 24.8% 3.7% 10%, 50% 0.25 73.3% 23.9% 0.2% 2.6% 26.7% 6.3% 10%, 100% 0.25 71.4% 23.3% 0.2% 5.2% 28.6% 8.7% 10%, 100% 0.4 69.2% 22.6% 0.2% 8.0% 30.8% 11.4% 30%, 100% 0.4 69.0% 22.5% 0.5% 8.0% 31.0% 11.8%

The mean white-dwarf mass is 0.59 M☉; white dwarfs heavier than 0.8 M☉ (progenitors > 3.7 M☉) are 3.3–3.5% of the total. The "heavier than the tracers" column is black holes + neutron stars + those heavy white dwarfs.

Dickson+2023 state that white dwarfs contribute ~30% of the total mass at ~10 Gyr for a canonical IMF, consistent with this calculation; a Codex calculation with a fixed 15 M☉ black-hole mass gives 25–40% for all remnants.

Left: present-day mass fractions of all remnants, white dwarfs and black holes against the black-hole retention fraction (Kroupa IMF, 12.5 Gyr, neutron-star retention 10%, no stellar escape). Right: the mass that can be more concentrated than the ~0.8 M☉ tracers, against the fractions our models need (horizontal lines) and the published omega Cen black-hole fractions (arrows).

docs.title: Which remnants can be more concentrated than the light
docs.text:
Mass segregation sorts objects by individual mass. The stars that trace the light in our data (F625W < 19 HST counts, G < 17 Gaia counts) are turnoff and giant stars of ~0.8 M☉. A typical white dwarf of 0.55–0.6 M☉ is heavier than a low-mass main-sequence star but lighter than these tracers, so after relaxation it should be less concentrated than the light, not more. Young white dwarfs have been observed diffusing outward in 47 Tuc (Heyl+2015). In omega Cen the white-dwarf sequence is split, interpreted with ~0.55 M☉ normal-population and ~0.46 M☉ helium-rich-population white dwarfs (Bellini+2013).

The component that can sit inside the light is therefore black holes, neutron stars and the heavy tail of white dwarfs. A large total white-dwarf budget does not justify a large compact component on top of the light.

docs.title: Retention and dynamical evolution
docs.text:
Natal kicks. Young pulsars have a Maxwellian kick distribution with a one-dimensional dispersion of 265 km/s (Hobbs+2005). For a remnant born at rest in a cluster with escape speed \(v_{\rm esc}\), the retained fraction is

\[ P_{\rm ret}={\rm erf}\!\left(\frac{v_{\rm esc}}{\sqrt2\,\sigma_k}\right) -\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{v_{\rm esc}}{\sigma_k}\,e^{-v_{\rm esc}^2/2\sigma_k^2}, \]

which gives 0.3–3.6% for σ_k = 265 km/s and v_esc = 60–140 km/s (omega Cen's present central escape speed is 63 km/s, Baumgardt+2019; it was higher in the past). Standard kicks retain few neutron stars in massive clusters: even forming neutron stars in binaries retains ~5% in the standard model of Pfahl+2002 (1–8% across their parameters), which motivates low-kick channels; many models adopt 10% (e.g. Hénault-Brunet+2020 for 47 Tuc). Black-hole kicks are reduced by fallback, which depends on the explosion mechanism and metallicity (Fryer+2012).

Dynamical evolution changes the fractions in both directions.

  • Preferential escape of low-mass stars raises the remnant fraction without adding remnant mass: dissolving clusters become remnant-dominated (Baumgardt & Makino 2003); present-day mass functions correlate with relaxation time and dark-remnant fraction (Sollima & Baumgardt 2017, Baumgardt & Sollima 2017).
  • A retained black-hole subsystem heats the cluster and changes which objects escape (Breen & Heggie 2013). Dynamical masses of Milky Way globular clusters exceed their stellar masses by more than a factor of 2, which N-body models reproduce only with low black-hole natal kicks (Rostami-Shirazi+2025).
  • Black-hole fractions can grow large: Palomar 5 may hold ~20% of its present mass in black holes after losing most of its stars (Gieles+2021).
  • Top-heavy IMFs raise remnant production but also early mass loss and disruption (Haghi+2020); multimass fits favour high-mass IMF slopes compatible with canonical values (Dickson+2023).

The remnant fraction is therefore not arbitrary at fixed IMF, stellar normalisation and history, but there is no history-independent ceiling well below unity.

docs.title: Omega Cen: published remnant content
docs.text:
Study Method Remnant content Zocchi+2019 two-component limepy (black holes vs other stars and remnants) black holes 4.5 (+4.0/−2.5)%, 1.35×10⁵ M☉ (Table 2) Baumgardt+2019 N-body grid, IMF and stellar evolution supply the remnants black holes 4.6 ± 0.5%, 1.65×10⁵ M☉; compatible with stellar-evolution predictions Dickson+2024 multimass limepy with IMF, IFMR and retention black holes 5.9 ± 0.2%, 1.82×10⁵ M☉ (12,400 black holes); all dark remnants 50.3% (Table 1; statistical errors only) Dickson+2026a (preprint) multimass models coupled to cluster evolution black holes ~8.3%; omega Cen is excluded from their sample relations as an outlier Dickson+2026b (preprint) as above, several black-hole prescriptions black holes ≳ 7% under each prescription Bañares-Hernández+2025 Jeans + pulsar accelerations; extra component on top of the light 2.65×10⁵ M☉ in a 1.88 pc Plummer (9.0%) Evans+2022 axisymmetric Jeans a compact remnant core can supply up to ~5×10⁵ M☉ (model-based, not a universal limit)

A stellar-mass black-hole binary has been detected directly (Whitaker+2026), which establishes that black holes exist in the cluster, not their total mass. For comparison, 47 Tuc holds only 430 (+386/−301) M☉ in black holes (Hénault-Brunet+2020) while its multimass models favour a large white-dwarf population (Dickson+2024): a small black-hole fraction does not mean little remnant mass.

How models treat remnants. Multimass equilibrium models (limepy; validated against N-body by Peuten+2017) need component masses supplied by a population model: Hénault-Brunet+2020 and Dickson+2023/2024 derive them from fitted mass-function slopes, an IFMR and retention, with segregation tied to object mass. N-body grids (Baumgardt+2019) and Monte Carlo models (Kremer+2020) generate them from the IMF and stellar evolution. Zocchi+2019 and Bañares-Hernández+2025 instead fit the dark component's mass and check it against population expectations, as our models do.

docs.title: Our models against these bounds
docs.text:
DF base model (best fit) Jeans comparison model (J-Trager) Extra component Plummer, 2.73×10⁵ M☉, a = 2.18 pc Plummer 5.4×10⁵ M☉, a = 5.3 pc, + black hole 4.25×10⁴ M☉ (posterior medians) q = M_rem/M★ (Jeans: including the black hole) 0.09 0.22 (median) to 0.34 (maximum likelihood) Fraction of the total 8.4% 17.9% (median), 25.5% (maximum likelihood) Remnant half-mass radius / stellar half-mass radius (10.4 pc) 0.27 0.66 Against the IMF budget heavier than the tracers (8.7–11.8%) inside, at high black-hole retention 1.5–2.9× above Against published black-hole fractions (4.5–8.3%) 1.0–1.9× (consistent once heavy white dwarfs and neutron stars, ~3–4%, are added) 2–6× Verdict physically sensible as black holes + neutron stars + heavy white dwarfs not plausible as remnants alone; more likely absorbs a radial M/L trend of its fixed light profile

The other fits. The tied, completeness-corrected DF refit (best fit 2.00×10⁵ M☉, a = 1.88 pc) has q = 0.065 and 6.1% of the total (3.28×10⁶ M☉), inside the IMF budget and the published black-hole fractions. The Jeans twin with the star-count tracer (J-counts) has 8.4×10⁵ M☉ in remnants plus a 3.67×10⁴ M☉ black hole (posterior medians): 27.9% of the total, q = 0.39 (32.2% and 0.47 at maximum likelihood), further above the budget than J-Trager. Across these four fits M_rem ranges from 2.0 to 8.4×10⁵ M☉ with χ²_kin between 152 and 190, so it is weakly constrained.

The Jeans model's remnant mass would require strong preferential loss of low-mass stars on top of full black-hole retention. Its broad 5.3 pc scale also suggests it is compensating for the fixed light-profile tracer, which our own mass-function measurement shows is not mass-follows-light (the mass per bright star rises outward).

docs.title: Proposed priors
docs.text:
From the Codex research pass (regularising, not published limits) and the IMF budget above. Not adopted: changing the priors changes the model.

Quantity Prior Reasoning \(q=M_{\rm rem}/M_\star\) HalfNormal(σ = 0.10), truncated at 0.30 95% below q ≈ 0.19; favours the literature scale, keeps a tail IMF-tied alternative q ≲ 0.13 (≲ 0.2 allowing for stellar depletion) heavier-than-tracer budget for a Kroupa IMF with full black-hole retention \(x=a_{\rm rem}/r_{h,\star}\) ln x ~ N(ln 0.3, 0.8²), 0.03 < x < 0.77 remnant half-mass radius below the stellar one; black-hole subsystems need not be extremely compact (Breen & Heggie 2013) Total remnant fraction (if modelled separately) f_R ~ N(0.40, 0.12²), 0.15–0.70 must apply to embedded plus extra remnants together

Both models' scales satisfy the scale prior. The DF mass (q = 0.09) sits near the centre of the mass prior; the Jeans mass (q ≈ 0.2) is in its tail.

The physically consistent alternative is a multimass model in which the remnant inventory and its radial distribution are predicted from the IMF, the IFMR, retention and depletion, normalised to the star counts, instead of a free Plummer added to a single light-following component.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• A black-hole subsystem and an IMBH are not mutually exclusive: the fast-moving stars require a point mass ≥ 8,200 M☉ (Häberle+2024), and an IMBH of ~5×10⁴ M☉ can grow in evolutionary models of omega Cen (González Prieto+2025).
  • The Dickson+2026 values are preprints.
  • Our extra component's mass trades against M★ (±23% on mocks); a q-prior constrains that trade but does not remove it.

Sources: the papers linked above (all in the SciX library); Codex research pass 2026-10-15; comparison of remnant masses and scales with published fits: Remnant mass and spatial scale.

docs.title: Base model fits
docs.text:
The reference result of the project: the base no-DM model (two-transition action DF for the stars, a Plummer remnant component, no dark matter, no central black hole) fitted jointly to 89 kinematic bins and the HST and Gaia star counts.

Since 2026-10-16 the reference DF fit is the tied, completeness-corrected refit (results/df/dftie_restart_20261016; objective 295.77, χ²_kin 159.4; best fit M_★ 3.08×10⁶ M☉, M_rem 2.00×10⁵ M☉, a_rem 1.88 pc). Its predictions differ from the 2026-10-13 fit below by a few per cent, but M_rem falls by 27 %: the split between stars and remnants is weakly constrained. The black-hole fits (DF + central black hole) and the figures below use the 2026-10-13 fit; the dark-matter fits use the tied refit.
