  • The same as before. The earlier profile scan in ρ20 (2026-09-23, old count likelihood with free amplitudes; plots/rho20_profile_20260923.png) found the same: the free halo went to ρ20 = 0, and fixing ρ20 = 1 cost +2.2 in the objective.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Uncalibrated errors. χ² per bin is about 1.6–2.1 in every model, so the published errors do not describe the scatter and Δln L is not calibrated. Mock fits with an injected halo are needed before an upper limit can be quoted.
  • Part of the gain relies on the outermost Gaia bins. These sit near 40 pc, where stars escaping the cluster and the Galactic tide may raise the dispersion. A halo is one way to fit them, not the only one.
  • Model differences. The Jeans and DF models differ in more than the halo: the anisotropy family, the treatment of the stellar mass, and the black hole (free in the Jeans models, absent here in the DF).

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
• Jeans halo twins. bin/run_jeans_counts_tracer.py BATCH --source rung2_K2_{nfw,cored}_turnover, run on 1 thread each; 2.5 h and 2.3 h.
  • DF halo fit. bin/run_compact_df_recovery.py prepare-real ... --branches free_halo --hand-starts 2 --start-from results/df/dftie_restart_20261016::observed_no_halo_start0 --counts ocen_counts_hst_f625w19_c,ocen_counts_gaia_g17_c --count-tie data/processed/kinematics/ocen_counts_tie_c.json, with the other options as in the tied refit.
  • Figures and numbers. bin/plot_jeans_dm_fits.py; numbers in results/plot_data/jeans_dm_fits_20261016.json.

docs.title: Jeans comparison model: no dark matter, free black hole
docs.text:
The best no-DM model of the earlier Jeans ladder (rung 2, results/fits/rung2_K1_turnover; the cored-halo rung2_K2_cored_turnover has a higher ln Z, 87.12 against 85.96; see dark-matter fits). It is shown as the dashed curve in the base-model figures and is the reference for the question of a central black hole. It is fitted to the same 89-bin kinematic snapshot as the DF base model, so the kinematic χ² of the two compare directly.

Status

Completed 2026-09-21 (nested sampling, 15,972 posterior samples). Current: it uses the same 89-bin kinematic snapshot as the DF base model and its likelihood replays exactly; the 2026-10-13 count-likelihood fix does not apply to it, because it uses a fixed light profile as its tracer, not the star counts. Physically consistent outside the central ~0.2 pc; inside, the standard separable DF construction fails (below).

docs.title: Model definition
docs.text:
Jeans equation. For a spherical tracer of density \( u(r)\) in a mass profile \(M(<r)\) with anisotropy \( eta(r)\),

\[ rac{d( u\sigma_r^2)}{dr}+ rac{2 eta}{r} u\sigma_r^2=- u rac{GM(<r)}{r^2}, \qquad u\sigma_r^2(r)= rac{1}{g(r)}\int_r^\infty g(s)\, u(s) rac{GM(<s)}{s^2}\,ds, \]

with \(g(r)=\exp\left(2\int^r eta/t\,dt ight)\). The line-of-sight and radial and tangential proper-motion dispersions follow from the standard projection integrals (Binney & Mamon 1982, 1982MNRAS.200..361B; van der Marel 1994, 1994MNRAS.270..271V) and are averaged over each bin as for the DF. The published rotation is subtracted from the model's second moments exactly as in the DF fit. Solver: src/ocen_dm/kinematics/jeans.py.

Tracer. Fixed, not fitted: an 11-component multi-Gaussian expansion of the composite light profile (oMEGACat star counts inside 25″, Trager+1995 outside; fit residual 0.18 mag rms), deprojected spherically.

Mass components.

Component Form Parameters Stars mass follows the MGE light \(M_\star\) Remnants Plummer sphere \(M_{ m rem}\), \(a_{ m rem}\) Black hole point mass at the centre \(M_{ m BH}\) Dark matter none —

docs.title: How the stellar mass is determined
docs.text:
• One stellar parameter, \(M_\star\): the mass normalisation of the fixed light profile, i.e. the stellar mass-to-light ratio. The stellar density shape is the MGE and is not fitted.
  • The anisotropy parameters do not change the density. They describe the stars' velocities only (unlike in the DF, where they also shape the density).
  • \(M_\star\) is set by the kinematics, jointly with the remnants, the black hole and the anisotropy; it is not taken from photometry.
  • Mass-to-light ratio. With L_V = 1.16×10⁶ L☉ (Harris V = 3.68, E(B−V) = 0.12, at the fitted distance), \(M_\star/L_V\) = 2.0 at maximum likelihood and 2.3 at the posterior median; \(M_{\rm tot}/L_V\) = 2.7–2.8, the same as the DF base model (2.8).

Anisotropy ("turnover"). Three levels joined by two smooth transitions (src/ocen_dm/kinematics/anisotropy.py):

\[ \beta(r)=\beta_0(1-f_1)+\beta_{\rm mid}(f_1-f_2)+\beta_\infty f_2, \qquad f_i=\frac{r^2}{r^2+r_i^2},\quad r_2=r_1+\Delta r . \]

The weights are non-negative and sum to one, so β never leaves the range of its three levels.

docs.text:

Fit: χ²_kin = 190.0 for 89 bins at maximum likelihood (DF base model: 156.4); ln Z = 85.96. Sampler: UltraNest, 400 live points, Δln Z = 0.5, slice steps 2 × ndim, seed 42.

The upper bound of the β₀ prior is physical, not empirical: a cored tracer around a point mass has a non-negative distribution function only if β₀ ≤ −½ (An & Evans 2006). The posterior piles up against that bound.

docs.title: Mass components
docs.text:
(a) Enclosed mass by component (Jeans: posterior median and 16–84% from 300 saved draws; DF base model dashed). (b) Circular velocity. (c) Non-stellar share of the enclosed mass. Grey: outside the radial range of the data.

  • The black hole dominates the centre. It holds more than half of the enclosed mass out to 1.3 pc; the stars and remnants inside 0.3 pc add only ~560 M☉. The circular velocity therefore rises towards the centre (Keplerian, 43 km/s at 0.1 pc), whereas in the DF model it falls to zero.
  • Beyond ~3 pc the two models agree on the total mass to within a few per cent (Jeans 3.24×10⁶ M☉ in total, posterior median of M★ + Mrem + MBH; DF 3.27×10⁶, best fit) and on the circular-velocity peak (~27–28 km/s near 9 pc).
  • They split the non-stellar mass differently. The Jeans model puts 5×10⁵ M☉ in a Plummer of 5.3 pc plus the 4×10⁴ M☉ black hole; the DF puts 2.7×10⁵ M☉ in a Plummer of 2.2 pc. At 10 pc the non-stellar share is ~23% (Jeans) against 15% (DF).

Physical plausibility of the remnant mass: 18–26% of the total including the black hole, 1.5–2.9× the IMF budget for remnants heavier than the tracers; see Remnant mass and the stellar population.

docs.title: Anisotropy
docs.text:
β(r) of the Jeans model (posterior median, 16–84% and 2–98% from 3,000 draws; transition radii r₁ and r₂ dotted) against the DF base model (dashed). Shaded: radial ranges of the HST/MUSE and Gaia data.

  • Inside ~1 pc the models differ in sign. The Jeans model is tangential (β ≈ −0.52 at the centre, −0.48 at 0.3 pc, −0.20 at 1 pc), as the black hole requires; the DF core is isotropic.
  • Between 3 and 15 pc they agree: mildly radial, peaking at β ≈ +0.15.
  • Outside ~20 pc both turn tangential; the Jeans model more strongly (−0.67 at 100 pc against −0.53), where only the Gaia data constrain it.

docs.title: Posterior and degeneracies
docs.text:
Posterior of the black-hole mass and the parameters it trades against (15,972 samples; dashed lines: 16, 50 and 84%).

  • M_BH is well bounded within this model: 4.25×10⁴ M☉, 95% interval 3.6–4.9×10⁴; no posterior sample is below 10⁴ M☉.
  • β₀ is pinned at its bound (−0.525, +0.019/−0.042), so the black-hole mass is measured conditional on the most radial central anisotropy the model allows.
  • M_BH correlates with the remnant scale and r₁ (correlation +0.53 and +0.51): a more extended remnant component or a larger tangential core needs a heavier black hole.
  • The leading degeneracy is stars against remnants (M_rem–M★ −0.95, M_rem–a_rem +0.94), the same stars-versus-dark-mass trade seen in the DF fits.

docs.title: Central bins
docs.text:
Bins inside 2 pc: HST radial and tangential proper-motion dispersions and MUSE line-of-sight dispersions, with the Jeans (solid) and DF (dashed) predictions and residuals.

Data inside 2 pc Bins χ² Jeans χ² DF HST PM radial 13 21.5 22.3 HST PM tangential 13 16.7 23.1 MUSE line of sight 17 20.8 19.4 Total 43 59.0 64.8
  • The black hole gains Δχ² ≈ 6 in the central 43 bins, almost entirely from the tangential proper motions inside 0.3 pc, where the data rise to 0.81–0.86 mas/yr and the DF stays at 0.76.
  • It overshoots the tangential dispersions at 0.4–1.4 pc (residuals −1 to −2.5σ), and the MUSE dispersions do not discriminate.
  • Over all 89 bins the DF fits better than J-Trager by Δχ² = 34, mostly at 2–20 pc (the J-counts twin, χ² 152.2, fits better than the DF's 156.4); see Comparison with the Jeans model.

docs.title: Physical consistency
docs.text:
Checks from the DF consistency audit, which tests necessary conditions for a non-negative stellar distribution function (passing them is not a proof that one exists):

Check Result Spatial density of every component non-negative everywhere Central condition with a black hole and a cored tracer, β₀ ≤ −½ met (enforced by the prior; β₀ = −0.503) Separable DF, first derivative (B₁) passes everywhere Separable DF, radial condition (R₂) passes everywhere Separable DF, second derivative (B₂) fails at 0.02–0.18 pc (minimum −0.11 at 0.12 pc); 89.7% of posterior draws fail in the same region
  • Outside the central ~0.2 pc no failure is found.
  • Inside it, the standard separable construction gives no non-negative DF. A non-separable DF with the same density and dispersions is not excluded, so the model is not shown to be unphysical there, only not shown to be physical.
  • That region is where the black hole dominates the mass and where its evidence comes from (the central bins above), which is why the result matters for the black-hole question.
  • The DF base model is non-negative by construction.

docs.title: What this model says about a black hole
docs.text: Within the Jeans framework the central rise of the HST proper-motion dispersions is fitted by a 4×10⁴ M☉ point mass with tangential central orbits. The evidence is local (Δχ² ≈ 6 from a few bins inside 0.3 pc), it depends on an anisotropy forced to its physical limit, and in the central ~0.2 pc, where the black hole acts, the standard separable construction of a non-negative distribution function fails. A point mass with a self-consistent DF has since been tested (DF + central black hole, 2026-10-15, fixed masses): objective 275.2 at 8,200 M☉ and 279.7 at 4×10⁴ M☉ (280.7 without); the 4×10⁴ M☉ cusp fits the central kinematics better but over-predicts the central HST counts. Not yet tested in the DF framework: radially biased orbits in the core and mass segregation of the remnants.

docs.title: Twin model with the star-count tracer (J-counts, 2026-10-16)
docs.text:
This model is identical to the one above (call it J-Trager) except for its tracer: the same 89 bins, 10 parameters, priors and sampler (400 live points). Only the multi-Gaussian expansion (MGE) is replaced. It was fitted to the completeness-corrected HST (2–250″) and Gaia (300–2400″) star counts, with their amplitude ratio tied to the measured value (count ratio). The MGE fits both count sets: HST deviance 20.5 over 20 bins, Gaia 13.5 over 12. Run: results/fits/jeans_K1_turnover_counts_c.

Kinematic data with each model's best fit, and residuals, for line-of-sight dispersion, radial PM (HST ●, Gaia □) and tangential PM. Top right: the two tracer profiles, J-counts divided by J-Trager. Bottom right: enclosed mass (posterior medians).

Scripts: bin/fit_count_tracer_mge.py, bin/run_jeans_counts_tracer.py, bin/plot_jeans_tracer_twins.py.

The count tracer. Top: the completeness-corrected HST counts, and the Gaia counts times the fitted ratio, with the 12-Gaussian MGE (solid). Dashed: the composite (Trager) MGE of J-Trager, scaled to the HST counts. Bottom: data / MGE − 1. Dashed: composite MGE / count MGE − 1.

J-counts posterior. These figures come from the same script as for J-Trager. Here the DF comparison is the tied DF refit, not the base fit.

Script: bin/plot_jeans_comparison_model.py --name jeans_K1_turnover_counts_c --jeans results/fits/jeans_K1_turnover_counts_c --df results/df/dftie_restart_20261016::observed_no_halo_start0.

Quantity J-Trager J-counts χ² of the best fit (89 bins) 190.0 152.2 HST PM radial / tangential (21 + 21 bins) 61.8 / 36.6 30.5 / 50.1 MUSE LOS (29) 51.7 49.8 Gaia PM radial / tangential (9 + 9) 16.9 / 23.0 10.7 / 11.2 ln Lmax; ln Z 121.1; 86.0 ± 0.3 140.0; 103.9 ± 0.5 M★ 2.67 (2.49–2.85)×10⁶ 2.28 (2.09–2.48)×10⁶ Mrem; arem 5.4 (3.8–7.0)×10⁵; 5.28 pc 8.4 (6.8–10.1)×10⁵; 5.13 pc MBH 4.25 (3.92–4.58)×10⁴ 3.67 (3.30–4.02)×10⁴ β0, βmid, β∞ −0.53, 0.19, −0.81 −0.52, 0.19, −0.86 D 5.361 kpc 5.362 kpc

Ranges are 16th–84th percentiles; the other values are posterior medians.

  • The tracers differ by 5–50 %. Relative to J-Trager, the count tracer is up to 7 % higher at 10–100″ and 5–10 % lower at 200–600″. Beyond 1000″ it is up to 50 % higher; there the Trager profile has no data and the MGE is an extrapolation.
  • The kinematic fit improves by Δχ² = −38 with the same number of parameters. The gain comes from the HST radial PMs at 100–400″ (−31) and both Gaia PM components (−18). It is partly offset by the HST tangential PMs (+13). The kinematic curves differ only slightly (see the residual panels). The kinematics are fitted at a level comparable to the DF base model (χ² 156–159).
  • The mass split shifts, but the total hardly changes. M★ falls by 15 % and Mrem rises by 57 %; the total (M★ + Mrem + MBH, posterior medians) is 3.16×10⁶ against 3.24×10⁶ M⊙.
  • MBH moves down by 14 % (1.3 posterior σ), and is still non-zero at high significance.
  • Caveat on the evidence. Δln Z = +18 between the two tracers is not a model comparison: the tracers are fixed inputs taken from different data, not fitted parameters.

Dark-matter fits of both Jeans models and of the tied DF refit: Dark-matter fits.

docs.title: Codex agama point mass 2026 10 15
docs.text:
The scaled-energy hypothesis is not supported as stated. AGAMA explicitly handles \(\Phi(0)=-\infty\): its coordinate [ X=\log[1/\Phi(0)-1/E] ] then becomes \(\log(-1/E)\). There is no automatic compression of weak binding energies caused by an infinite central potential. The grid is adaptive in log radius. See scaleE, actions_spherical.cpp:42, createInterpolationGrid, potential_utils.cpp:738, and the upstream implementation.

Also, your frequency mode named "exact" still trusts finite, bound mapper outputs without checking their action residual. It inverts \(J_r(E,L)\) only for nonfinite or unbound outputs. Accurate quadrature at the wrong energy remains a possible error. regularized_df.py:119

A. AGAMA has a direct route, but neither suggested option guarantees your required accuracy.

  • ActionFinder(potential, interp=False) does not disable spherical interpolation. The factory selects ActionFinderSpherical without consulting interpolate; that argument reaches the axisymmetric branch only. actions_factory.cpp:35
  • agama.actions(potential, points) selects direct spherical integration automatically. No method argument is needed. It dispatches to evalSpherical, which computes energy from the supplied potential, finds turning points, and integrates \(J_r\). interface_python.cpp:3724, actions_factory.cpp:20, actions_spherical.cpp:585
  • Direct does not mean arbitrarily accurate. Its quadrature order is capped at 40, with a heuristic documented for approximately constant accuracy down to \(r_p/r_a=10^{-3}\). That is inadequate assurance for your extreme eccentricities. actions_spherical.cpp:30, math_core.h:560

I checked the installed binary in pure Kepler, \(M=8200\), \(J_r+L=100\):

\(L/(J_r+L)\) agama.actions relative \(J_r\) error ActionFinder error 0.001 \(+4.49\times10^{-4}\) \(+3.61\times10^{-4}\) 0.01 \(-1.42\times10^{-5}\) \(-1.07\times10^{-3}\) 0.3 \(+8.78\times10^{-13}\) \(-4.05\times10^{-7}\)

interp=False reproduced the default finder. Thus the \(4.5\times10^{-4}\) Kepler error also exists without action interpolation.

There are nevertheless concrete interpolation failure mechanisms worth investigating:

  • The finder computes energy using its internal interpolated potential, rather than the original composite. Your comparison therefore mixes potential-interpolation and action-interpolation errors. actions_spherical.cpp:649
  • It interpolates \(J_r/(L_c-L)\), clips coordinates to its table boundaries, and clamps negative results to zero. This provides a mechanism for spurious zero actions, although I have not established which mechanism caused your start-2 failure. actions_spherical.cpp:337, actions_spherical.cpp:73
  • The mapper extrapolates its energy table and applies one first-order correction. That is not a converged action inversion. actions_spherical.cpp:679, actions_spherical.cpp:725

B. Establish an all-direct BH reference before adopting a hybrid.

I would first use converged direct \(J_r\) quadrature throughout BH models. Use that implementation to determine where approximation is safe. Replacing only weakly bound actions prematurely assumes the error depends primarily on energy; the eccentricity dependence above already contradicts that simplification.

Your existing helper needs hardening before becoming a general action backend: it assumes r0 lies inside the orbit, uses fixed-order quadrature, and clips negative radicands. Require valid brackets, explicit radial/circular limits, and convergence checks rather than treating every returned number as certified. regularized_df.py:179, regularized_df.py:213

For a production hybrid:

  • Validate an error envelope over energy, circularity, and allowed potential parameters, including actual velocity quadrature nodes.
  • Choose the boundary from errors in density, pressures, projected predictions, and likelihood—not an arbitrary radius.
  • A hard switch is acceptable if the disagreement is negligible throughout the overlap. Otherwise moving model parameters can move quadrature nodes across a finite jump. Smooth blending removes that jump but does not remove bias or guarantee monotonic actions.

Your velocity nodes are fixed in escape-speed fraction, so their physical energies change with the potential; a fixed Gauss rule does not eliminate this switching problem. positive_df.py:157

If direct evaluation is too expensive, your own table is reasonable. However, AGAMA already uses Kepler-compatible scaled energy and circularity coordinates. The improvement must be validated table construction, refinement, and fallback, rather than merely choosing those coordinates again. actions_spherical.cpp:347

C. Small action errors can matter, but their magnitude alone cannot establish fit bias.

For your implemented exponential DF, at fixed amplitude, [ \delta\log f \simeq -\alpha(L_c/J_0)^\alpha\,\delta L_c/L_c. ] Errors can therefore be amplified in the steep tail. A relative error in \(J_r\), especially near \(J_r=0\), is not directly a relative error in dispersion. regularized_df.py:438

The decisive test is:

  1. In the same frozen potential and DF, replace only the action calculation; compare density, both pressures, and actual bin predictions.
  2. Rebuild self-consistency with each backend and compare the full objective.
  3. Refit representative starts and the BH-mass profile; measure parameter shifts and likelihood changes.

Use the joint prediction displacement [ D^2=\sum_i(\Delta\sigma_i/s_i)^2+ \sum_j(\Delta\mu_j)^2/\mu_j ] as an initial diagnostic, then evaluate the actual likelihood with its nuisance parameters treated consistently. The implemented objective combines kinematic residuals and count deviances; count normalizations and backgrounds may be profiled. df_fit.py:130, counts.py:155

For scale: a coherent dispersion shift of \(0.1\%\) across 89 independent bins with \(2\%\) errors gives \(D^2\approx0.22\). That does not imply a \(0.1\%\) action error produces that shift.

D. The main diagnostic traps are these.

  • Mapper frequency agreement can hide wrong actions. In Kepler the frequency ratio is independent of energy. In composites, verify the returned \(J_r(E,L)\) and actual angular momentum before trusting a bound mapper point. Your current fallback does not perform those checks. regularized_df.py:127
  • Export corruption extends beyond the BH. This AGAMA version writes analytic component types without their parameters. Plummer reconstruction defaults include mass=1, scaleRadius=1. Reloading can therefore change remnants as well as remove the point-mass singularity. Reconstruct every static component from configuration and verify potential/force equality before comparison. potential_factory.cpp:995, potential_factory.cpp:1032, potential_factory.cpp:158
  • rmax is not an orbit boundary. Multipole evaluates an asymptotic continuation outside its grid. Direct integration there can accurately measure the continuation rather than establish its physical accuracy. Test radial-domain convergence separately. potential_multipole.cpp:1478

  • Current validation shares the suspect backend. Closure uses self.af, and GalaxyModel receives that same finder; direct projected moments therefore do not independently validate actions. The BH action regression checks agama.actions only for \(c>0.1\) and \(q<10^5\), excluding the reported difficult regime. regularized_df.py:605, positive_df.py:338, test_regularized_df.py:318

  • Verified versus assumed. I read the cited project and local AGAMA sources, checked that the relevant local AGAMA source files match those shipped with the installed package, and ran read-only numerical comparisons. Your radial quadrature recovered the sampled Kepler actions accurately and exposed the direct-routine eccentricity errors above. I did not reproduce the base/start-2 failures, orbit integrations, or full fits. I assume your reported observations and uncertainties are accurate. The available AGAMA environment lacks SciPy, so I did not run the project suite.

  • Strongest argument against my recommendation. All-direct evaluation may impose substantial cost for errors that largely cancel in integrated observables. A validated hybrid could deliver indistinguishable inference much faster. The missing evidence is the full prediction-and-refit comparison, not further isolated action accuracy.

  • Checks needed for confidence. Confirm the actual fitting binary/version; reproduce start-2 from the live potential; separate internal-potential error from action-table error; establish quadrature convergence in composite potentials; test finite-but-wrong mapper outputs; verify export/reconstruction force equality; and compare rebuilt models, refits, and BH profiles against the direct reference.

docs.title: Codex central counts research 2026 10 15
docs.text: Research mode used: ordinary Codex web research fallback Native Deep Research: unavailable from this invocation path Scientific source rules: yes Model effort: high Date: 2026-10-15

docs.title: 1. Executive summary
docs.text:
• I found no published oMEGACat-specific artificial-star calibration giving absolute completeness at F625W = 19–21 in the central few arcseconds. The catalogue paper’s completeness comparisons establish improved depth, but do not supply the recovery fractions needed to correct your bins. Häberle et al. 2024, oMEGACat II.
  • A marginal central underdensity is documented. Anderson & van der Marel explicitly report fewer stars near the centre than around 10″, after completeness correction. Their companion paper finds the innermost counts compatible with a flat core. This is not an established physical depletion of bright stars. Anderson & van der Marel 2010; van der Marel & Anderson 2010, §4.
  • The weight of resolved-star evidence favours a flat or very shallow projected density profile over a securely detected cusp. The historical cusp claim depended on a centre displaced by approximately 12″ and on unresolved-light measurements. Modern fast-star evidence and a central velocity-dispersion rise concern kinematics, not a newly established number-density cusp. Noyola et al. 2008; Häberle et al. 2025.
  • An IMBH does not require an observable Bahcall–Wolf cusp in the bright-star counts. Relaxation, stellar masses, cusp extent, projection, and the DF determine the prediction; recent omega Cen simulations produce a stellar density slope near 1.3. González Prieto et al. 2025, Appendix A.3.
  • Your counts challenge the specified \(4\times10^4\,M_\odot\) DF more strongly than the no-BH model. Explaining the discrepancy entirely through missing stars would require approximately 43% and 54% completeness in the two bins. The literature does not establish incompleteness this severe for this bright selection.

docs.title: Completeness: what has actually been published?
docs.text:
For the HST oMEGACat catalogue, a quantitative central recovery calibration remains unverified. In oMEGACat II, §VII.1 compares magnitude histograms and radial source densities between catalogues. I found no artificial-star experiment, tabulated \(C(m,R)\), or prescription specifically validating core number-density profiles. The official collaboration page lists the catalogue and subsequent releases, but supplies no such calibration itself.

There are relevant cautions:

  • KS2 cannot measure saturated stars; the team supplements its measurements with hst1pass photometry.
  • Bright stars can have only one short-exposure measurement in F435W or F625W, so requiring multiple measurements can remove otherwise useful stars.
  • Astrometric precision worsens below approximately F625W = 17.5 as saturation affects more exposures. This is not a statement that those stars disappear from the catalogue.
  • The example photometric selection rejects the lowest QFIT decile in magnitude bins and requires \(o<0.5\). These are quality selections, not completeness corrections. Häberle et al. 2024, §§VI.6, IX.2.

The commonly quoted Nitschai completeness numbers refer to MUSE spectroscopy relative to an HST parent catalogue:

Source Verified result Applicability Nitschai et al. 2023, oMEGACat I For GO spectroscopy with S/N \(>10\), overall completeness reaches 50% at F625W = 18.86; fainter-star completeness is poorer centrally. Spectral extraction completeness, not HST detection completeness. Nitschai et al. 2024, oMEGACat III Selecting F625W \(<17\) gives \(>80\%\) completeness in all fields and approximately 90% in most. Supports their bright-RGB population analysis; does not certify F625W \(<19\) HST counts at 2–3″.

These are measured selection/recovery fractions, not confidence limits. Nitschai et al. 2023, §III.2; Nitschai et al. 2024, Appendix A.

Earlier HST artificial-star tests do exist. Anderson & van der Marel ran 500,000 tests, including over 700 within 1″ and over 51,000 within 10″. One central \(15″\times15″\) example recovered 3,402/3,847 = 88%; their profile bins had \(>80\%\) completeness even centrally. These results use their older reduction and F435W instrumental selections; they cannot be assigned directly to your oMEGACat F625W bins. Anderson & van der Marel 2010, §§3.5, 5.1.

A useful 2026 addition is Chen et al.’s JWST artificial-source testing in a central \(2″\times2″\) box: 56,000 injections per NIRCam filter and 42,000 per MIRI filter. Their 50%-recovery magnitude differs by approximately two magnitudes between favourable and unfavourable positions. This demonstrates strong local crowding variation, but calibrates JWST infrared detections, not oMEGACat F625W completeness. Chen et al. 2026, §IV.

docs.title: What do the central density profiles show?
docs.text:
Here distinguish [ n(r)\propto r^{-\gamma},\qquad \Sigma(R)\ \text{or}\ I(R)\propto R^{-\Gamma}. ] The historical observed slopes below are projected slopes.

Noyola, Gebhardt & Bergmann 2008: a shallow light cusp. Their ACS F435W integrated-light profile rises inward with [ \Gamma=0.08\pm0.03. ] The paper reports this slope uncertainty without specifying its confidence convention in the accompanying paragraph. Their adopted centre came from sector-based star counts. Spherical isotropic modelling gave [ M_\bullet=4.0^{+0.75}{-1.0}\times10^4\,M\odot ] at 68% confidence, excluding zero BH at \(>99\%\) under those assumptions. Thus both the photometric cusp and mass inference were conditional on their centre and measurement method. Noyola et al. 2008, §§2, 4 and Fig. 5.

Anderson & van der Marel 2010: flat counts, with a marginal depression. Their completeness-corrected profiles show no sharp central rise. They write that the

“density in the centermost bins appears smaller (at marginal significance)”

than around 10″. Their adopted star-count centre is [ \alpha=13^{\rm h}26^{\rm m}47.24^{\rm s},\quad \delta=-47^\circ28′46.45″, ] with approximately 1″ uncertainty per coordinate, independently supported by kinematics. The reconstructed Noyola centre is 12.3″ away. They attribute the apparent unresolved-light enhancement largely to bright-star PSF wings and shot noise. Anderson & van der Marel 2010, §§4–5, 8.

Van der Marel & Anderson 2010: the fitted shallow cusp is not a central detection. Their global generalized-Nuker fit gives \(\Gamma=0.05\pm0.02\), a formal 1σ error. But fitting only \(R\leq15″\) gives [ \Gamma=0.00\pm0.07\quad(1\sigma). ] They interpret \(\Gamma\lesssim0.07\) as an approximately 1σ upper limit: the \(\Gamma=0.05\) model overpredicts both innermost points by about 1σ and is preferred because it fits better near 10″. Their spherical anisotropic Jeans analysis yields \(M_\bullet\lesssim1.2\times10^4\,M_\odot\) at approximately 1σ, or \(1.8\times10^4\,M_\odot\) at approximately 3σ, allowing core and shallow-cusp alternatives. van der Marel & Anderson 2010, §§4, 6–7.

Noyola et al. 2010: renewed kinematic evidence, rather than an independent density-cusp measurement. VLT/FLAMES integrated spectra gave a central dispersion of \(22.8\pm1.2\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}\)—the quoted measurement error—and a kinematic centre approximately 3.5″ from Anderson & van der Marel’s. Spherical isotropic fits produced BH masses of approximately \(3.0\)–\(5.2\times10^4\,M_\odot\) depending on centre; this is a range across centre choices, not a confidence interval. The paper’s \(\Delta\chi^2=1\) curves provide the formal one-parameter 1σ errors. Noyola et al. 2010, §§3–4.

docs.title: Modern centre and IMBH results
docs.text:
Pechetti et al. 2024 find counter-rotation inside approximately 20″. Their preferred rotation centre is \(13^{\rm h}26^{\rm m}47.31^{\rm s},-47^\circ28′51.39″\), with approximately 1.5″ RA and 5″ Dec uncertainties, estimated from a joint 1σ \(\Delta\chi^2=2.3\) map. Other methods perform worse because the core is flat and the kinematics complex. This is not a precise replacement for the star-count centre. Their spectroscopy found no significant central high-velocity outliers, a result subsequently overtaken in depth by the HST proper-motion search. Pechetti et al. 2024, §§5–6.

Häberle et al. 2024, Nature identify seven fast stars within 3″, with five forming the robust subset. Assuming they are bound and the background cluster escape speed is 62 km s\(^{-1}\), their combined projected positions and velocities require approximately \(8,200\,M_\odot\). This is a conditional dynamical minimum, not a stated 95% or 99% interval. Its minimum-mass location lies 0.3″ from the Anderson–van der Marel centre.

Their acceleration-plus-velocity Bayesian analysis gives \(M_\bullet>21,100\,M_\odot\) at 99% confidence, with spatial priors and assumed bound orbits. These results do not establish a bright-star density cusp. Their 65.2% quality-cut pass fraction within 90″ is likewise not an artificial-star completeness measurement. Use the corrected coordinates and equation in the revised paper. Häberle et al. 2024, Methods; 2024 correction.

Häberle et al. 2025, oMEGACat VI measure a central dispersion near 0.81 mas yr\(^{-1}\), approximately 21.1 km s\(^{-1}\) at their adopted distance. A smooth global Gaussian fit leaves a central dispersion excess inside 10″. Its fitted centre is offset by [ (\Delta{\rm RA},\Delta{\rm Dec})=(-1.31\pm0.72,\,+1.44\pm0.66)″ ] from the photometric centre. These are the quoted fit errors; §IV.2 does not explicitly state their confidence convention. The paper supports the same central vicinity but does not publish a new completeness-corrected number-density cusp. Häberle et al. 2025, §§III.2, IV.2.

González Prieto, Rodriguez & Cabrera 2025 provide particularly relevant modelling. Their two highlighted evolutionary models reach 47,000 and 51,000 \(M_\odot\) after 12 Gyr; these are simulation outcomes, not observational confidence bounds. They reproduce the broad brightness and dispersion profiles, while predicting a slightly brighter inner core. Their stellar 3D mass-density slopes settle near \(\gamma\simeq1.3\), versus approximately 1.97–2.1 for stellar-mass BHs. The \(\gamma=1.75\) cusp elsewhere in their appendix belongs to an equal-mass benchmark, not their present-day omega Cen stellar population. González Prieto et al. 2025, §III.1 and Appendix A.

Contradictory mass evidence remains. Bañares-Hernández et al. favour an extended \(2\)–\(3\times10^5\,M_\odot\) component with scale radius 1.5–2.2 pc, reporting these ranges at 3σ, and an IMBH upper bound of \(6,000\,M_\odot\) at 3σ. Their spherical Jeans model allows both extended remnants and a point mass. It uses older proper-motion data rather than jointly fitting the individual oMEGACat fast stars; its inferred background escape speed is approximately 10% higher. Thus its apparent conflict with the fast-star minimum involves different potentials and data, not merely incompatible formal error bars. Bañares-Hernández et al. 2025, §§3, 6, 8.3.

I could not verify a relevant Evans et al. 2025/2026 central-density paper. The verified Evans, Strigari & Zivick study is 2022, based on axisymmetric kinematic modelling; it is not a new innermost star-count measurement. Evans et al. 2022.

docs.title: What density profile should an IMBH produce?
docs.text:
Relaxed, equal-mass limit. The Bahcall–Wolf solution has [ f(\mathcal E)\propto\mathcal E^{1/4},\qquad n(r)\propto r^{-7/4}, ] requiring collisional relaxation in a BH-dominated potential. A pure extended power-law component projects to \(\Sigma\propto R^{-3/4}\). This is an equilibrium theoretical result, not a universal profile for every IMBH host. Bahcall & Wolf 1976.

Multiple stellar masses. In the classical weak-segregation solution, lighter tracers approach \(r^{-3/2}\) while the heaviest component is steeper. Bright RGB/SGB stars are therefore not interchangeable with the total mass distribution, especially if stellar-mass BHs dominate central scattering. The precise slopes depend on the mass spectrum and component abundances. Bahcall & Wolf 1977.

Finite-action DF: a separate route to \(r^{-3/2}\). Your model can generate this cusp without having reached Bahcall–Wolf equilibrium. If an isotropic DF tends to a finite, nonzero value \(f_0\) as the actions vanish, then in the Keplerian asymptotic regime [ n(r)\simeq\frac{4\pi}{3}f_0 \left(\frac{2GM_\bullet}{r}\right)^{3/2}. ] This is a phase-space-volume argument. “Finite” alone is insufficient: a DF tending to zero can behave differently. Collisionless adiabatic growth of a BH in an initially isothermal core gives the same \(r^{-3/2}\) asymptote. Quinlan, Hernquist & Sigurdsson 1995.

A three-dimensional cusp can look nearly cored. Projection adds stars along the entire sightline through omega Cen’s much larger core. The asymptotic relation \(\Gamma=\gamma-1\) applies to a sufficiently extended pure cusp; it need not describe the total profile across a small transition region. Realistic cluster simulations already demonstrated shallow projected bright-star slopes of approximately −0.1 to −0.3, despite an IMBH and central mass segregation. Baumgardt, Makino & Hut 2005.

Heating and scouring require a dynamical history. IMBH-driven energy generation can maintain a large cluster core. A hard BH binary can additionally eject central stars and destroy a cusp; subsequent relaxation can regrow it. Merritt & Szell’s simulations find regeneration over roughly one relaxation time, extending to approximately \(0.2r_{\rm infl}\). Those simulations concern galactic nuclei: they establish a mechanism, not evidence that omega Cen’s central bright stars were scoured. A stationary point mass by itself does not prescribe a deficit. Merritt & Szell 2006.

docs.title: Angular scales and the expected observable signal
docs.text:
At \(D=5.4\) kpc, 1″ = 0.02618 pc. Using the explicit convention \(r_{\rm infl}=GM_\bullet/\sigma_{\rm 1D}^2\), with an illustrative \(\sigma_{\rm 1D}=22\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}\), I obtain:

\(M_\bullet\) \(r_{\rm infl}\) Angular radius \(8,200\,M_\odot\) 0.073 pc 2.8″ \(20,000\,M_\odot\) 0.178 pc 6.8″ \(40,000\,M_\odot\) 0.355 pc 13.6″ \(50,000\,M_\odot\) 0.444 pc 17.0″

These are calculated scales, not statistical constraints. The proposed 0.07–0.3 pc range is plausible for particular dispersions or influence-radius definitions, but its upper end is not universal.

The observable cusp can occupy only a fraction of this radius. Consequently, a low-mass IMBH could have its strongest density signature mostly inside your bins, whereas a \(4\times10^4\,M_\odot\) model should be tested directly at 2–3″. Neither slope nor excess-star count follows from BH mass alone.

docs.title: Interpretation of your counts
docs.text:
The following calculations use your supplied counts and predictions, without inspecting local data.

Radius Observed \(4\times10^4\,M_\odot\) DF Observed/predicted No-BH DF Observed/predicted 2.00–2.55″ 6 14.1 0.426 10.8 0.556 2.55–3.24″ 12 22.1 0.543 17.5 0.686 Combined 18 36.2 0.497 28.3 0.636

The quoted probabilities are correctly lower-tail Poisson probabilities, \(P(N\leq N_{\rm obs}\mid\lambda)\): 0.01338 and 0.01438. For the no-BH predictions they are 0.0872 and 0.1116.

Pooling the two bins gives \(P(N\leq18\mid36.2)=0.000643\), compared with 0.0266 for \(\lambda=28.3\). These are conditional tail probabilities for fixed predictions and a preselected region—not global rejection significances after fitting, choosing bins, varying the centre, or accounting for completeness uncertainty.

Three implications follow.

  1. A 10–15% correction cannot by itself reconcile the bright counts. If missing stars explain everything, the BH model requires approximately 57% and 46% losses in those bins. Even the no-BH model requires approximately 44% and 31% losses. Thus the discrepancy is partly shared by both models.

  2. Flat magnitude ratios constrain differential completeness, not absolute completeness. They argue against a large additional loss confined to one bright slice. They permit a common spatial loss, centre-induced flattening, or a shared tracer deficit. If the reported ratios average broadly over \(R<10″\), the diagnostic is weaker still: your two annuli occupy only 6.5% of that area.

  3. The tension concerns the DF’s central occupation as well as \(M_\bullet\). A finite, nonzero small-action DF imposes a particular cusp and normalization. Rejecting that prediction would not automatically reject an IMBH with a different tracer DF, segregation history, or depleted orbit population.

Removing quality cuts avoids one source of selection, but does not measure detection completeness or undo any requirements implicit in the parent catalogue’s construction.

docs.title: 3. Disagreements, uncertainties and open questions
docs.text:
What is established: a weak unresolved-light cusp was reported historically; completeness-corrected resolved counts instead support a core or very shallow cusp, with a marginal innermost depression. Modern kinematics provide substantial evidence for a compact central mass, while model-dependent mass estimates remain disputed.

What is not established: a statistically secure, selectively bright-star deficit in omega Cen caused by saturation, collisions, tidal destruction, or BH-binary scouring. The published marginal depression has not acquired a verified physical attribution.

For your specific discrepancy, the unresolved issues are:

  • Absolute local completeness: no verified oMEGACat recovery fraction presently justifies either assuming 100% or applying a factor-of-two correction at F625W \(<19\).
  • Centre uncertainty: approximately 1–2″ is consequential for these annuli. Predictions must be integrated around the same adopted centre as the data and marginalised over its uncertainty.
  • Spatial structure near bright stars: azimuthally averaged magnitude ratios can conceal small exclusion regions.
  • Tracer correspondence: the model must represent the exact magnitude-selected population, including its evolutionary phases and catalogue requirements.
  • DF flexibility: a physical IMBH test should allow alternatives to a nonzero constant small-action DF.

My assessment: the evidence supports describing your result as a central bright-tracer shortfall relative to the fitted DF, with a published marginal precedent. Calling it documented crowding incompleteness, or documented dynamical scouring, would go beyond the sources.
