docs.text: Claude verified the code findings (symmetry prefilter at 60", b at bound 5 for 120" fits, no convergence check) and that the brief misstated the symmetry results (21-23: +4.1, -3.8).

docs.title: Determining the centre of omega Cen (NGC 5139): critique a published kinematic centre and design a rigorous measurement
Context
docs.text: We model omega Cen's inner kinematics (Jeans and action-DF models, IMBH question). The adopted centre is Anderson & van der Marel 2010 (AvdM10, 2010ApJ...710.1032A): RA 13:26:47.24, Dec -47:28:46.45, from HST ACS star counts (isodensity contours and "pie slices"), confirmed within 1-2" by an HST PM kinematical centre and 2MASS unresolved light; quoted accuracy ~1". Goldsbury+2010 (2010AJ....140.1830G, ACS GC survey ellipse fits within 2'): +0.41" E, +0.35" N of AvdM10 (quoted 0.1"). Haeberle+2024 (Nature) IMBH position from fast-star accelerations: 0.77" NE of AvdM10.

docs.title: The published kinematic centre (oMEGACat VI, Haeberle+2025, 2025ApJ...983...95H, sec. 4.2), text quoted
docs.text: "we fit a 2D Gaussian function to velocity dispersion values determined in the Voronoi bins [vorbin, target 250 stars per bin, 2,434 bins, median uncertainty ~0.02 mas/yr]. A single 2D Gaussian provides a decent fit with a reduced chi2 = 0.99 and independently recovers the cluster center (dRA = -1.31 +- 0.72", dDec = 1.44 +- 0.66") with respect to the photometric center determined in AvdM10. The best-fit position angle is 101.4 +- 2.4 deg ... flattened ... 1 - sigma_y/sigma_x = 0.09 ... the residuals show that there is a significant rise of the velocity dispersion within r < 10". ... Allowing a second Gaussian component (with the same center as the first component) ... reduce[s] the reduced chi2 to 0.91. The kinematic center, the position angle, and the flattening of the outer component are still successfully recovered." Their PM catalogue (oMEGACat II, 2024ApJ...970..192H): 1.4 M stars to the half-light radius (~5'), F625W to ~25, PMs from ~20-yr HST baselines, LOCALLY CORRECTED: "this local approach to measure proper motions also removes any signature of rotation" (mean PM field ~0 everywhere; dispersions preserved). Partial energy equipartition is detected (sigma depends on stellar mass). The HST field is a mosaic of many programmes with varying depth/exposure. Separation from AvdM10: 1.95" (chi2 = 8.1 for 2 dof, p = 0.018); the authors call it "in agreement".

docs.title: Our own star-count centres (oMEGACat catalogue, all stars with F625W, x = dRA* east+, y = dDec, arcsec from AvdM10)
docs.text: HST coverage: every 3" cell occupied to R = 250" (C1 coverage >= 0.956 inside 250"). - Inside 60" the projected density changes by only ~15% (core radius ~140"), so the core alone fixes the centre to 1-5". - Symmetry (opposite wedges, 8 pairs, annulus 5-55"): consistent with 0 within +-2". - Unbinned Poisson fits of an elliptical cored power law Sigma ~ (1+m^2/a^2)^-b in circular apertures about AvdM10: R<120": F625W<19 (-3.1+-1.1, +1.9+-1.3); 19-21 (-0.8+-1.0, +1.0+-0.8); 21-23 (-1.8+-0.8, +0.9+-0.7); all<23 (-1.7+-0.6, +1.1+-0.4) R<200": F625W<19 (-4.0+-0.7, +1.0+-0.7); 19-21 (-2.4+-0.5, +1.0+-0.4); 21-23 (-1.8+-0.5, +0.3+-0.5); all<23 (-2.3+-0.4, +0.6+-0.2) (bootstrap errors, 20 draws; q and PA poorly constrained, b and a vary with aperture). - A PM rotation-field centre is impossible with these locally corrected PMs (mean tangential PM 0.001-0.008 mas/yr to 200"). - Motivation: about AvdM10, the bright stars (F625W<19) show a ~1.8-sigma central dip inside ~3" and a bump at 5-8"; fainter stars are flat (slope 0.00 +- 0.07 over 2-8.5"); about the oMEGACat VI centre nothing is seen. Data available locally: oMEGACat VI catalogue (RA, DEC, x, y, pmra/pmdec_corrected + errors, vlos + err for ~300k MUSE stars, f625w, f814w, quality/membership selections), Gaia DR3/EDR3 members (absolute PMs, sparse in the core), JWST NIRCam mosaics of the centre (GO 8322, 4343; bright stars saturated), HST raw data not reduced by us (no artificial stars).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. What are the assumptions behind the oMEGACat VI kinematic centre and how robust is it? Identify concrete failure modes (model shape vs the true sigma(R), asymmetric field footprint / depth, magnitude mix + equipartition, PM error under-estimation varying by field, Voronoi binning, local correction, rotation-projection plumes, counter-rotating core), and estimate how large a bias each could produce in arcsec.
  2. Is our star-count offset (~2" W, 1" N at R<200") independent evidence, or could it share systematics with theirs (same HST footprint and depth pattern)? What would distinguish a real large-scale centre offset (lopsidedness / m=1 mode, offset core vs envelope) from a systematic?
  3. Design a better, more rigorous centre measurement with this data: what likelihood (counts, dispersion, LOS rotation, combined?), what selection (magnitude-matched, completeness-limited, symmetric footprint), what nuisance terms (m=1 mode, radial-dependent centre, ellipticity), how to calibrate with mocks (injected offsets, realistic depth maps), and what precision is realistically achievable for (a) the core centre (R < 20") and (b) the global centre. Be critical and specific; give the expected precision with a short calculation.
  4. What is the right centre to use for (i) inner profile/dip tests, (ii) Jeans/DF modelling of the inner 10", (iii) the IMBH question? Should the centre be a nuisance parameter in the dynamical fits? Separate what you verified from what you assumed. Argue against your own recommendation once.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
The saved results contradict the packet’s claim that the wedge centres are all consistent with zero within ±2″. The faint-star result is (+4.09″, −3.81″), with a quoted x error of 0.74″, near the search boundary. That result needs investigation before using the symmetry test as corroboration. (results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:129, bin/hst_density_centre.py:43)

My recommendation is to retain AvdM10 as the reporting origin, treat the physical centre as uncertain, and fit centre coordinates jointly with the inner dynamics. Neither the published dispersion centre nor the present count fits establish a subarcsecond core centre.

  1. How robust is the published kinematic centre?

It estimates the centre of an empirical, approximately elliptical dispersion field. Interpreting that as the potential centre assumes that tracer populations, selection and measurement errors do not introduce an asymmetric dispersion pattern. The two-Gaussian fit imposes a common centre, so its agreement does not independently demonstrate that the inner excess and outer cluster are concentric. Reduced χ² near one tests average residual size, not bias in two particular parameters. oMEGACat VI, §4.2

The packet’s p=0.018 treats AvdM10 as exact. Adding an assumed independent 1″ uncertainty per coordinate for AvdM10 changes χ² from 8.07 to 2.57, giving p≈0.28. Thus “in agreement” is defensible; neither calculation establishes which centre is correct. The actual reference covariance and meaning of its quoted accuracy are needed.

The following are conditional sensitivity estimates, not measured biases. For illustration, take a dispersion gradient \(g_\sigma=10^{-3}\ {\rm mas\,yr^{-1}\,arcsec^{-1}}\). An unmodelled dipole of amplitude \(A_\sigma\) can mimic approximately \(A_\sigma/g_\sigma\) arcseconds. Actual responses require the fit’s spatial weights and nuisance-parameter covariance.

Failure mode Concrete mechanism and conditional scale Wrong radial profile A radial model error alone does not select a direction under symmetric sampling. If asymmetric weights convert 10–30% of a 0.01 mas/yr radial residual into a dipole, the shift is 1–3″. Footprint/depth Missing area alone need not bias a correctly specified conditional velocity likelihood. It changes the weighting of model errors and population mixtures. For counts, a 1–3% completeness dipole divided by a density gradient of 0.0065 arcsec⁻¹ mimics 1.5–4.6″. Magnitude mix/equipartition With \(\sigma\propto m^{-\eta}\), assumed \(\eta=0.09,\sigma=0.65\), a dipole of 0.05–0.2 in effective \(\ln m\) gives 3–12″. This is a stress test; the local mass mixture must be measured. Underestimated PM errors \(\Delta\sigma\simeq(e_{\rm true}^2-e_{\rm quoted}^2)/(2\sigma)\). Spatially asymmetric 10–20% error underestimation with quoted errors 0.05–0.15 mas/yr gives roughly 0.4–8″. Uniform underestimation changes the profile, not necessarily its centre. Voronoi bins Compare the model with the constituent stars, rather than just one bin coordinate. For illustrative bin widths 10–30″ and curvature scales 50–150″, the curvature error corresponds to approximately 0.03–0.8″; misplaced representative coordinates can contribute more. These bin sizes are assumptions. Local corrections Removing mean rotation does not guarantee independent, unchanged dispersions. The reduction uses overlapping reference sets and adds correction uncertainty. An unaccounted reference-noise difference between 50 and 150 stars gives about 4″ in a simplified mean-subtraction calculation. Correct accounting removes that particular bias; correlations can still enlarge uncertainty. oMEGACat II, §5.3 Rotation-projection plumes Symmetric paired plumes produce zero first-order translation bias with symmetric sampling. Ten-percent odd leakage of projected streaming variance for assumed \(V=3–5\) km/s and \(\sigma=20\) km/s corresponds to approximately 1–3″. Rotating radial/tangential axes alone preserves the covariance trace. Counter-rotating core A concentric reversal alone gives zero translation bias. Asymmetric unresolved streaming can produce the preceding scale; an actually displaced component shifts a common-centre fit according to its statistical weight. Counter-rotation should be allowed in the LOS mean model. Pechetti et al.

These effects overlap; adding those ranges in quadrature would be unjustified.

  1. Are the count offsets independent evidence?

They provide a different observable, but not an independent control of HST selection systematics. Your fit selects finite F625W and positions, then normalizes the density over an unmasked circular aperture. It contains no spatial completeness or depth term. (bin/hst_density_centre.py:65, bin/hst_density_centre.py:75, bin/hst_density_centre.py:93)

Occupancy is insufficient evidence for completeness: the footprint estimator marks cells occupied by any catalogue star and explicitly assigns full area inside 30″. A cell can contain many detections while missing a few percent of the relevant population. (bin/build_count_profiles.py:85, bin/build_count_profiles.py:99)

There are additional reasons to distrust the quoted count uncertainties:

  • Twenty individual-star bootstraps hold field selection errors fixed. Their estimated standard deviations themselves have roughly 16% sampling uncertainty. (bin/hst_density_centre.py:106)
  • The optimizer returns parameters without checking or saving convergence status. (bin/hst_density_centre.py:84)
  • Both faint and combined 120″ fits reach \(b\simeq5\), the imposed upper bound. That makes their errors conditional on a restrictive profile family. (bin/hst_density_centre.py:76; results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:164, :225)
  • The wedge search prefilters stars to 60″, although a 55″ annulus displaced by more than 5″ needs stars beyond 60″. The saved faint solution has a 5.6″ displacement, so a crescent of its trial annulus is unavailable. (bin/hst_density_centre.py:42, :52; results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:129)

A real offset should persist in common magnitude/colour populations, separate programmes, independent instruments, and symmetric masks. A systematic should track exposure boundaries, crowding, error distributions or photometric thresholds. Repeat fits in disjoint radial ranges to distinguish a common translation from an inner/outer displacement.

Crucially, a small translation produces [ \delta\ln\Sigma=-\boldsymbol{\delta c}\cdot\nabla\ln\Sigma. ] This is itself an \(m=1\) pattern. An arbitrary radial dipole and an arbitrary centre are therefore non-identifiable without an explicit convention or external constraint.

  1. A more rigorous measurement

I would use a marked spatial point-process likelihood with conditional stellar velocities:

[ \log L=\sum_i\log\lambda(\mathbf x_i,m_i,k_i) -\int_W\lambda\,dA\,dm +\log p({\mathbf v_i}\mid{\mathbf x_i,m_i,k_i}), ] where \(k_i\) identifies population or observing configuration, and \(\lambda=C(\mathbf x,m,k)\Sigma_k(\mathbf x)+\lambda_{\rm field}\).

Concrete choices:

  • Selection: use fixed sky apertures and a fixed mask containing diametrically opposite coverage. Fit narrow magnitude/colour slices with common support. For kinematics, retain quality cuts and model their selection; matching magnitude distributions alone does not match stellar masses across populations.
  • Counts: use a flexible monotonic radial profile, ellipticity and position angle; integrate selection over the actual window. Without artificial-star tests, constrain relative completeness through overlaps and independent imaging, then propagate uncertainty rather than declaring completeness from occupancy.
  • PMs: fit Cartesian components with their measurement covariance, mass dependence and spatial error-scale terms. Forward-model local correction effects and shared-reference covariance where possible.
  • LOS velocities: fit the mean and dispersion simultaneously, allowing rotation reversal, perspective effects, programme zero points and binaries. A solid-body mean field alone cannot determine both centre coordinates: one translation is degenerate with systemic velocity and the perpendicular coordinate is unconstrained.
  • Geometry: first fit one centre. Then test separately centred inner and outer components and constrained dipole terms. Define or regularize the dipole so it cannot freely reproduce a translation.
  • Combination: count positions and velocities conditional on those positions can be combined. Repeated binnings or overlapping magnitude samples are not additional independent observations.
  • Mocks: inject 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 5″ offsets into catalogues with realistic depth, crowding, mass mixtures, error fields, rotation and correction correlations. Include radial profiles outside the fitted family. Reapply selection and binning. Measure bias, interval coverage and false dip detections; use programme/spatial-block resampling as a complementary check.

Precision: distinguish a core measured locally from a centre extrapolated inward.

For a smooth core \(\Sigma\simeq\Sigma_0e^{-\alpha R^2}\), the stated 15% decline by 60″ gives [ \alpha=-\ln(0.85)/60^2=4.5\times10^{-5}\ {\rm arcsec^{-2}},\qquad {\rm SE}(c_x)\simeq\frac{1}{\alpha R_{\max}\sqrt N}. ]

The saved 60″ samples contain 86,075 combined and 13,481 bright stars. Assuming approximately constant central density gives \(N_{20}\approx9,600\) and 1,500. Thus R<20″ counts alone give about 11″ and 29″ per coordinate, even before completeness and profile uncertainty. These are illustrative Fisher limits, not confidence intervals. (results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:213, :30)

For the global counts, the saved 200″ models imply an approximate RMS logarithmic gradient of 0.0065–0.0070 arcsec⁻¹. Using [ {\rm SE}(c_x)\simeq\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt N\,g_{\rm rms}} ] gives 0.28″ combined and 0.66″ bright, conditional on the fitted circularized profile and known selection. The underlying model parameters and sample sizes are saved at results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:239 and :56.

A reasonable design target is 1–2″ total global uncertainty after calibration. Current results do not establish that accuracy. A distinct central dispersion excess could provide 1–3″ localization if, illustratively, \(N_{\rm eff}\sim1,000\) and \(|d\ln\sigma/dR|\sim0.01\) arcsec⁻¹; the two-component Gaussian Fisher estimate is about 2.2″ per coordinate. That locates the excess, not automatically the smooth stellar core.

  1. Which centre should enter the science?

  2. Dip tests: retain a predeclared reporting origin and marginalize over an independently estimated centre distribution. Do not select the centre that maximizes or removes the dip. The existing scan changes observed counts while retaining fixed model expectations, so it is a sensitivity diagnostic rather than a fitted-centre significance calculation. (bin/check_count_centre.py:51)

  3. Inner Jeans/DF fits: make centre coordinates nuisance parameters and recompute stellar radii, component projections and selection integrals. The current HST loader fixes these using OCEN_RA/DEC; the DF objective consumes already reduced radial data and count nodes. A new centre cannot be represented by simply shifting those radial coordinates. (src/ocen_dm/kinematics/hst_profile.py:125; src/ocen_dm/kinematics/df_fit.py:145, :164)
  4. IMBH inference: distinguish the cluster/potential centre from the compact object’s position. Fit their relationship explicitly and propagate astrometric registration uncertainty. The 0.77″ NE position is model-dependent: the 2024 paper reports accelerations individually consistent with zero within 3σ. Your plot additionally substitutes a 45° direction for “NE”; that marker is not a measured coordinate pair. Häberle et al.; bin/hst_density_centre.py:19, :36

Verified versus assumed. I verified the selection, likelihood normalization, search limits, bootstrap procedure, optimizer handling, saved results, fixed-centre projection and radial DF inputs cited above. The existing centre tests check catalogue-origin consistency and propagation, not recovery of a physical centre under asymmetric completeness; the count tests exercise amplitude recovery and integration. (tests/test_cluster_centre.py:25, :47; tests/test_counts.py:18, :91, :105)

The bias table, central-count extrapolation and achievable total precision are assumptions or analytical sensitivity calculations. I did not reproduce the catalogue fits or inspect the authors’ fitting implementation. Test execution was unavailable because the active Python lacks pytest; it also lacks NumPy/Astropy. Nothing was modified.

Strongest argument against my recommendation. A real common displacement remains plausible: all three disjoint 200″ magnitude slices lie west and north of the origin, and the combined result resembles the published dispersion offset. (results/plot_data/hst_density_centre.json:47, :108, :169, :230) Excessively flexible completeness and dipole terms could absorb that physical signal, while an AvdM10-centred prior could pull the answer back artificially. Report prior sensitivity and independently identifiable centre definitions.

What I would check before trusting the result:

  • Full published centre covariance, reference-centre uncertainty and RA-versus-RA* convention.
  • Actual bin averaging, fit weighting and centre stability under binning/profile changes.
  • Expanded wedge searches with sufficient input coverage; optimization convergence, slope-bound and quadrature checks.
  • Magnitude-dependent completeness and PM-error maps by programme, including local-correction covariance.
  • Independent HST/JWST/Gaia registration and population-matched comparisons.
  • End-to-end injected-offset coverage tests, including centre selection in the dip statistic and joint centre–IMBH inference.

docs.title: Codex cusp depletion 2026 10 15
docs.text:
The mass-budget premise needs correcting first: with proper renormalization, depletion redistributes the fixed \(M_\star\); it does not remove total stellar mass or require replacement by remnants. The amplitude is explicitly normalized to the requested mass. (regularized_df.py:519–525)

I recommend fixed \(p=4\), one free \(J_c\), as a conditional compatibility experiment. Include \(M_\bullet=0\), retain the undepleted branch, and test sensitivity to fixed smaller \(p\). Do not interpret this experiment as measuring a cusp slope, identifying a depletion mechanism, or establishing a black-hole mass.

A. Fixed \(p=4\) is adequate for the first experiment; free \(p\) is not yet justified.

For an isotropic Kepler limit, the asymptotic result is

\[ \rho(r)\propto \begin{cases} r^{-(3-p)/2},&0\le p<2,\\ r^{-1/2}\log(r_0/r),&p=2,\\ r^{-1/2},&p>2. \end{cases} \]

Thus \(\gamma=(3-p)/2\) cannot be extrapolated to \(p=4\). Increasing \(p\) above two changes the transition, not the limiting slope. The isotropic lower bound \(\gamma\ge1/2\) is consistent with An & Evans.

A three-dimensional \(r^{-1/2}\) cusp has finite central surface density and can look flat in projection. Whether its slope is sufficiently small between the actual observed radii depends on its amplitude, transition scale and surrounding cluster. Flat projected counts therefore neither require a three-dimensional core nor establish \(p=4\).

The alternatives have different interpretations:

  • Energy depletion: equivalent to action depletion in the unbiased pure-Kepler limit, since \(J_r+L=GM_\bullet/\sqrt{2\mathcal E}\). It offers no immediate identifiability advantage. Away from that limit, prefer \(D(L_c)\) because it preserves the existing contours; those contours depend on the potential and anisotropy prescription. (regularized_df.py:527–559)
  • A positive DF floor: restores the \(r^{-3/2}\) cusp sufficiently far inward. It can hide that cusp below resolution, but adds an unconstrained crossover.
  • A loss cone: suppresses low angular momentum at fixed energy, unlike suppression of low \(L_c\). Use it only for a specific destruction/scouring hypothesis and test the predicted tangential anisotropy. The distinction is explicit in the loss-cone treatment of González Prieto et al..
  • Relaxation or mass segregation: does not directly motivate \(p=4\). Relaxed light populations generally retain approximately \(r^{-3/2}\) cusps; heavier populations become steeper. A shallow depleted population instead needs an evolutionary explanation and a cusp-regrowth timescale. (Alexander & Hopman, Merritt)

Fit fixed \(p=4\), then repeat with, for example, \(p=0.4\) and \(p=1\). These span limiting slopes \(1.3\), \(1\), and \(0.5\) without simultaneously fitting two poorly separated shape parameters. Only free \(p\) if likelihood profiles and injections demonstrate that the observed radial range separates it from \(J_c\).

B. A depleted tracer can retain a dispersion rise; an upward mass shift is plausible, not compulsory.

In an isotropic, black-hole-dominated power-law region, Jeans gives

\[ \sigma_r^2=\frac{GM_\bullet}{(\gamma+1)r}. \]

Changing \(\gamma\) from \(3/2\) to \(1/2\) therefore increases local variance by \(5/3\) at fixed mass. Depletion preferentially removes tightly bound orbits; surviving stars passing through the centre can have high velocities.

Projection works in the opposite direction by reducing their contribution relative to foreground/background cluster stars. Under idealized asymptotic assumptions:

  • \(\gamma=3/2:\ \sigma_{\rm proj}^2\propto R^{-1}\);
  • \(\gamma=1/2\), with finite central \(\Sigma:\ \sigma_{\rm proj}^2\propto R^{-1/2}\).

The rise becomes shallower, but survives. These are analytical limits, not predictions for your finite bins. The implementation projects density and pressures separately, so changing their radial shapes changes both numerator and denominator. (positive_df.py:322–338)

Consequently, there is a mass–depletion degeneracy, but no universal monotonic rule \(J_c\uparrow\Rightarrow M_\bullet\uparrow\). Calculate the response in every central PM/LOS bin before refitting, then profile \(M_\bullet\) against \(J_c\). The supplied information cannot determine the mass shift quantitatively.

C. Keep Plummer remnants for the first comparison, but make the conclusion conditional on that choice.

A prescribed Plummer component is mathematically usable as an external gravitational source. It does not demonstrate a physically admissible remnant DF or collisional equilibrium; the implementation supplies its potential without constructing either. (regularized_df.py:648–654)

Also, your reported compensation is not an increase in central remnant density. From the saved parameters,

\[ \frac{\rho_{\rm rem,new}(0)}{\rho_{\rm rem,base}(0)} =\frac{503869}{273161}\left(\frac{2.180}{4.045}\right)^3 \simeq0.29. \]

The larger remnant mass is substantially more extended. (batch.json:362–363, summary.json:205–206)

Do not add freely adjustable stellar depletion and a freely adjustable remnant cusp simultaneously in the first experiment. Subsequently compare a specified concentrated-remnant alternative. The cited evolutionary models predict stellar and stellar-BH cusps with different slopes, supporting that sensitivity test. (González Prieto et al., Appendix A.3)

If depletion is meant to affect only the bright tracer through mass segregation, applying it to the entire self-gravitating stellar DF is an additional assumption. The current count likelihood uses the same model surface density, with a scalar amplitude per count product; it cannot represent a radial change in tracer-to-stellar-mass ratio. (df_fit.py:151–156)

D. The principal implementation risks are numerical, especially the escape shell.

  • Normalization: multiply the same depletion factor into the callable and normalization integrand. Evaluate it stably, handle \(J_c=0\) explicitly, and check integration-domain extension independently of order doubling. Both existing orders use the same finite domain. totalMass() repeats the normalization quadrature, so it is not independent spatial mass verification. (regularized_df.py:578–614)
  • Contour boundaries: retain direct integration outside the grid. Test continuity and derivatives at both boundaries; depletion introduces another action scale that can expose interpolation errors. (regularized_df.py:562–575)
  • Underflow cutoff: its high-action envelope remains valid for unchanged contours and \(0\le D\le1\), using the new normalized amplitude. Nonmonotonicity of the depleted DF does not invalidate that envelope. Never add a hard low-action cutoff. (regularized_df.py:595–608)
  • Action guard: the claim that an overestimated action can only remove mass becomes false for a nonmonotonic depleted DF. The guard recomputes finite actions beyond 300 pc only when their approximate DF is positive; finite errors inside that radius remain unchecked. Compare against exact actions across the depleted family, including erroneous actions landing near its zero or maximum. (regularized_df.py:294–318)
  • Escape shell: fixed speed quadrature can miss the finite-binding-energy stars dominating a strongly depleted central population. In a Kepler potential their fractional speed-shell width shrinks roughly as \(r/r_{\rm depletion}\). Agreement between two inadequate orders is insufficient. Use an independent binding-energy/adaptive integration reference. The production rule integrates directly in \(v/v_{\rm esc}\), while equilibrium closure checks density only. (positive_df.py:162–180, regularized_df.py:759–774)

Use separate undepleted jobs and positive, preferably logarithmic, \(J_c\) starts. Near \(J_c=0\), \(p=4\) gives a weak response that can defeat finite-difference optimization. The driver uses fixed steps in normalized coordinates and resumes saved coordinate vectors, so use fresh batches when changing the parameterization. (run_compact_df_recovery.py:503–510, run_compact_df_recovery.py:583–588)

E. Retaining the tension is defensible; cutting at \(3''\) is only a sensitivity test.

A \(3''\) cut cannot remove a discrepancy extending through \(13''\). Report excluded-bin predictions and compare masses using identical retained datasets. The centre diagnostic covers eight bins from \(2''\) to approximately \(13''\), using fixed model expectations without refitting. (check_count_centre.py:40–56)

Flat magnitude ratios also cannot exclude incompleteness shared by all slices; the diagnostic explicitly admits that ambiguity. (check_hst_count_completeness.py:4–7)

  1. Verified versus assumed.

I verified the implementation issues above and inspected the saved refits. Both stop on ftol, with reported optimality approximately 25 and 55; both pass numerical validation but fail the configured data-fit criteria. These are candidate fits, not established global minima. (8200 summary:112–115, 40000 summary:112–115, 8200 gates:1314–1344, 40000 gates:1314–1344)

I did not rerun tests, refits or catalogue diagnostics. I assume the packet’s empirical completeness and centre summaries are accurate. The asymptotic calculations assume spherical equilibrium and the stated isotropic Kepler limit; their applicability at observed radii remains unverified. Nothing was modified.

  1. Strongest argument against my recommendation.

Fixed \(p=4\) imposes the shallowest isotropic asymptote and may manufacture compatibility through an extreme tracer choice. The evolutionary alternative with \(\gamma\simeq1.3\) could yield a materially different mass conclusion. An improved objective could therefore demonstrate model flexibility while weakening physical interpretability. The published \(\gamma\simeq1.3\) result is a stellar mass-density fit over \(0.001\)–1 pc, not a direct prediction for your magnitude-selected counts. (González Prieto et al., Appendix A.3)

  1. Minimum checks needed before trusting refits.

  2. Exact legacy recovery at \(J_c=0\), schema/optimizer round-trips, positivity, origin behavior and stable extreme-parameter evaluation. Existing tests assert an undepleted, nonzero origin; that does not validate depletion. (test_regularized_df.py:25–54)

  3. Independent Kepler density and pressure benchmarks spanning \(p<2\), \(p=2\), \(p>2\), including shell resolution and projected asymptotes. The existing constant-DF benchmark does not exercise this regime. (test_regularized_df.py:209–220)
  4. Independent action-space normalization, spatial mass closure, exact-action rebuilds, contour-boundary checks, and convergence of every count expectation and dispersion bin.
  5. Multiple starts and numerical/Jacobian sensitivity checks at all three masses; then profiles in \((M_\bullet,J_c)\) and fixed-\(p\)/remnant alternatives.
  6. Repeated noisy injections, including undepleted truth, depleted truth and mismatched tracer/remnant families, before interpreting significance or coverage. Existing mocks supply Gaussian dispersion noise and Poisson counts but remove streaming, so they do not validate streaming systematics. (compact_recovery.py:44–64)

docs.title: Codex df point mass 2026 10 15
docs.text:
The scratch patch leaves incorrect finite-centre assumptions in place: the frequency ratio is forced to 2 at \(L=0\), and the spline enforces the corresponding boundary derivative. With a point mass, the \(L\to0^+\) frequency ratio is 1. Bypassing the guard therefore does not establish a correct BH extension. (regularized_df.py:95–128, regularized_df.py:147–158)

My recommendation: proceed as a conditional compatibility experiment, but change the depletion coordinate, fix the radial boundary, and validate observables before fitting. This is more than a 30-line production change.

  1. What \(D(q)\) actually does. It suppresses small total action, rather than all low-angular-momentum orbits. A radial orbit with large \(J_r\) survives. Away from a Kepler potential, \(q\) is not an energy coordinate, so multiplication changes the angular weighting of the existing DF; its original contour construction does not prevent that. The implementation explicitly distinguishes \(q\) from its contour label \(L_c\). (regularized_df.py:225–233, regularized_df.py:260–283)

For example, in a harmonic core, [ E-\Phi(0)=\Omega(2J_r+L),\qquad q=\frac{E-\Phi(0)}{2\Omega}+\frac L2. ] At fixed energy, increasing \(D(q)\) favours larger \(L\). Thus it can introduce tangential bias and a central density depression even without a BH. It does not necessarily empty the centre: finite-action stars still pass through it.

The small-action slope also needs correction. In an isotropic Kepler control, writing positive binding energy as \(\mathcal E\), [ q=\frac{GM_\bullet}{\sqrt{2\mathcal E}},\qquad f\sim q^p\sim\mathcal E^{-p/2}, ] and [ \rho=4\pi\sqrt2\int_0^\psi f(\mathcal E) (\psi-\mathcal E)^{1/2}\,d\mathcal E. ] Consequently, [ \rho(r)\sim \begin{cases} r^{-(3-p)/2},&0\le p<2,\ r^{-1/2}\log(r_0/r),&p=2,\ r^{-1/2},&p>2. \end{cases} ] The proposed quadratic depletion is the logarithmic borderline, not a pure \(r^{-1/2}\) cusp. Every nonzero \(J_c\) has that same limiting behaviour; \(J_c\) changes where the transition occurs. These are analytical deductions, consistent with the isotropic bound in An & Evans.

Renormalization is mandatory: include the same depletion factor in both the callable DF and its action integral, then recompute the amplitude during every potential rebuild. Currently those expressions contain only the exponential. Merely multiplying the returned DF changes the requested stellar mass. (regularized_df.py:217–223, regularized_df.py:276–305)

  1. Form I would choose. Use depletion in \(L_c\). With zero anisotropy bias and correct frequencies, that preserves the energy contours; multiplying by \(D(q)\) generally does not. A function of \(L_c\) also preserves the existing contour derivative ratios wherever its derivative is nonzero. This follows from the characteristic equation used to construct \(L_c\). (regularized_df.py:177–179, regularized_df.py:225–233)

For an initial one-parameter compatibility screen, I would use [ D(L_c)=\frac{(L_c/J_c)^4}{1+(L_c/J_c)^4}, ] with an explicit \(J_c=0\) branch returning 1, and compare against the undepleted model. Call \(J_c\) a depletion scale.

If the objective is to infer the asymptotic slope, free \(p\), with \(\gamma=(3-p)/2\) for \(0\le p<2\). Freeing both \(p\) and the transition scale requires two parameters. No single scale parameter independently controls both quantities. Neither scalar depletion represents a loss cone or permits an intrinsically flat isotropic stellar core around a BH.

  1. Numerical risks.

  2. Fix both the radial frequency boundary and the spline boundary. Replacing only the frequency assignment leaves the spline enforcing the wrong condition. (regularized_df.py:128, regularized_df.py:147–158)

  3. The dangerous velocity regime is the thin shell near escape speed: after strong high-binding depletion, stars with finite binding energy dominate the central density. The fixed Gauss–Legendre speed rule can miss that shell. Density closure alone does not certify pressure accuracy: the closure check extracts only density, while the observable table subsequently uses the nominal velocity order. (positive_df.py:157–175, regularized_df.py:447–461, regularized_df.py:468–471)
  4. Outside the action lookup grid, evaluation integrates contours directly; normalization nevertheless covers a finite action interval. Doubling node counts does not enlarge that interval or change r_min. Test domains separately from resolution. (regularized_df.py:260–284, compact_recovery.py:95–109)
  5. The unresolved stellar cusp is continued using the fitted innermost logarithmic slope. Vary r_min and check its enclosed mass and force; an integrable cusp does not automatically imply an accurate continuation. (positive_df.py:180–199)

  6. Add explicit finite-value checks to final closure diagnostics: the regularized constructor uses threshold comparisons that do not themselves reject NaNs. (regularized_df.py:452–462)

  7. Identifiability. Taking the supplied influence radii and radial coverage as assumptions, \(8200\,M_\odot\) is marginally resolved; \(4\times10^4\,M_\odot\) should affect more bins. That supports testing compatibility, not assuming either mass is identifiable.

Profile \(M_\bullet\) against depletion scale, anisotropy, stellar mass, remnant mass/scale and distance. Counts constrain tracer shape but do not independently fix stellar mass when their amplitudes are profiled—the saved base fit uses free count amplitudes. (df_fit.py:153–156, summary.json:183–202)

Require repeated noisy injections at \(0,\ 8200,\ 40000\,M_\odot\), spanning depletion and remnant alternatives. Measure false exclusions, mass bias and interval coverage. The existing mock generator supplies Gaussian dispersion noise and Poisson counts, but deliberately drops streaming; it is not by itself a test of streaming-systematic robustness. (compact_recovery.py:31–64)

  1. Fixed Plummer remnants. Acceptable as a declared first sensitivity case; insufficient for a robust BH measurement. The component is prescribed gravity with no remnant DF, so stellar self-consistency establishes nothing about remnant equilibrium. (regularized_df.py:339–343, regularized_df.py:415–423)

Missing concentrated remnant mass could be assigned to the BH, although refitting can change the direction of the final bias. Bracket plausible centrally concentrated remnant profiles before quoting a BH constraint. A specific relaxed remnant cusp requires additional physical assumptions.

  1. Engineering beyond the DF expression.

  2. Persist and validate \(M_\bullet,J_c\) in configuration. The scratch BH lives in a mutable global outside cfg, so its serialized configuration cannot reproduce the potential. (packet:2546–2566)

  3. Add fitting coordinates and starting values explicitly: the driver constructs a fixed coordinate list, rejects unknown bound overrides, and copies only named parameters for --start-from. (run_compact_df_recovery.py:175–181, run_compact_df_recovery.py:290–317, run_compact_df_recovery.py:900–905)
  4. Handle zero boundaries deliberately; logarithmic coordinates exclude zero. (df_fit.py:183–201)

  5. Fix mass accounting: mass_profiles()["total"] sums stars, remnants and halo only. Its recovery metrics could therefore validate a “total” that omits the BH. Also extend diagnostics below the current 0.5-pc reporting minimum. (compact_recovery.py:112–141, run_compact_df_recovery.py:489)

  6. Simpler experiment. First correct point-mass support and refit the original DF at fixed \(M_\bullet=0,\ 8200,\ 40000\,M_\odot\), without depletion. Then add \(D(L_c)\) and repeat with matched nuisance freedom. Finally profile BH mass and calibrate conclusions with injections.

The baseline already fails its own data-fit gates: \(\chi^2_{\rm kin}=156.39\) for 89 points, HST count deviance \(96.92\) for 20 bins, and data_fit_passed=false. Numerical validation passes. Therefore a relative fit improvement alone is insufficient evidence for a calibrated BH constraint. (summary.json:1199–1241)

Separately:

  1. Verified versus assumed. I verified the implementation, configuration/driver paths, cited tests and saved baseline diagnostics by reading them. I did not execute tests or reproduce the scratch results. The regularized test currently requires BH rejection; the existing Kepler moment test exercises the separate DoublePowerLaw branch. (test_regularized_df.py:91–92, test_positive_df.py:73–94) The cusp scaling is my derivation under the stated isotropic Kepler assumptions. The supplied influence radii and physical remnant-response picture remain assumptions.

  2. Strongest argument against my recommendation. The scientific question concerns resolved bins, not the mathematical origin. The radial-boundary defect and \(D(q)\)-induced angular changes might be negligible at observational precision. If corrected and uncorrected implementations give indistinguishable bin predictions, the original quadratic proposal could suffice for a narrow compatibility test. Its positivity is not the problem; interpretation and demonstrated accuracy are.

  3. Checks needed to be sure. Require pure-Kepler frequency/action round trips across eccentricity; \(L_c=J_r+L\) and isotropy controls including the radial boundary; the derived \(p<2,\ p=2,\ p>2\) density limits; exact old-model recovery at both new parameters zero; independent action-mass normalization; separate radial-domain, velocity, contour and projection convergence; direct AGAMA projected-moment comparisons at actual selection nodes; and noisy BH recovery under alternative remnant/anisotropy models. Use Baes & Dejonghe as an analytic numerical benchmark, supplemented by the shallow-cusp controls above. Also require saved-config replay to reproduce the BH force and reported total mass.

docs.title: Codex mass model next 2026 10 13
docs.text:
The proposed r_s ≥ 10 pc cut does not establish the physical separation you claim. For the implemented cored halo, neglecting the distant taper, the half-density radius is only \(0.260\,r_s\): a 10 pc scale still permits a roughly 2.6 pc core. It therefore does not automatically eliminate remnant-like concentration. regularized_df.py:325

My recommendation: correct and validate the count likelihood first, then build a constrained multi-mass pilot using mass-resolved photometry and PMs. Continue reporting conditional enclosed-mass sensitivity curves meanwhile. Several independently flexible DFs would be premature.

a) Which next step, and what is minimally useful?

There is a correctness issue upstream of the proposed model expansion. Count-profile nodes are quantiles of the observed stars’ radii, and predicted density is averaged equally over those nodes. Expected annular counts instead require integrating density over the footprint and completeness function. build_count_profiles.py:54, counts.py:146

For a complete annulus sampled from the correct density, the current average approaches \(\int\Sigma^2\,dA/\int\Sigma\,dA\), whereas the required average is \(\int\Sigma\,dA/A\). This systematically overweights dense regions. My analytic check gives a 1.96% excess for \(\Sigma\propto R^{-2}\) across the adopted HST logarithmic bin width. That is an illustrative calculation, not a measurement of the actual fit bias. build_count_profiles.py:122

The mocks repeat the same averaging prescription while retaining the observed nodes, so successful recovery cannot expose this error. compact_recovery.py:55

After that correction, use:

  • Two or three observed stellar-mass bins, plus an extrapolated low-mass population and a separate WD population; retain a phenomenological NS/BH component initially.
  • A shared DF family with mass-dependent action scale and a small number of segregation parameters. Do not give every bin independent shape and anisotropy freedom.
  • Joint radial counts by mass bin and PM dispersions by mass and radius, with selection-specific tracer predictions.

Mass-resolved PMs supply useful additional information about segregation; they do not independently fix unseen low-mass stars, WD retention, or DM. There is already directly relevant omega Cen evidence: oMEGACat VI measures PMs over approximately 0.29–0.69 \(M_\odot\), finding weak, radially varying partial equipartition and different radial/tangential behaviour. Do not impose full equipartition. arXiv:2503.04903

Verified literature matches:

Reference Relevant method or correction Baumgardt & Hilker 2018 — 1804.08359 N-body grids fitted to density, kinematics and available stellar MFs. Gieles & Zocchi 2015 — 1508.02120 Self-consistent single/multimass LIMEPY models. Zocchi, Gieles & Hénault-Brunet 2018 — 1806.02157 Omega Cen: remnant populations and anisotropy can mimic central dark-mass signatures. Hénault-Brunet et al. 2019 — 1810.05167 Mock M4 method comparison, including a minimal three-component model. Hénault-Brunet et al. 2020 — 1908.08538 47 Tuc multimass inference with variable MF and remnant content. Watkins et al. 2022 — 2206.05300 Mass-dependent HST PM dispersions and partial equipartition. Evans, Strigari & Zivick 2022 — 2109.10998 Axisymmetric dynamical modelling, not a multimass LIMEPY application.

b) Is r_s ≥ r_half defensible?

As an explicitly conditional “extended halo” hypothesis, yes. As a necessary physical prior, no. Absence of stellar mass segregation in particle DM does not imply this radius inequality. Baryonic contraction and stellar heating can both alter DM concentration; neither supplies a universal cutoff at the stellar half-mass radius. arXiv:1104.2548

Nor does “non-segregated” uniquely identify DM. WD masses overlap the stellar mass range, and their distribution need not resemble a compact NS/BH subsystem. The photometric calculation itself assumes a mean WD mass of 0.55 \(M_\odot\). build_mass_function.py:63

Report \(M_{\rm DM}(<r)\) at several radii, alongside total mass and total unseen baryonic-plus-DM mass. This improves parameter interpretation; it cannot resolve an unidentified decomposition. Enclosed component masses are already calculated. compact_recovery.py:112

c) What makes the architecture easy or hard?

  • Existing foundation: MassLightDFModel already separates gravitating mixture weights from tracer weights and clears cached moments when reweighting. However, it uses the older DFModelConfig/DoublePowerLaw components and produces one combined tracer. Its strictly positive light fractions also prohibit a truly invisible component within that mixture. df_mass_recovery.py:95, df_mass_recovery.py:140, positive_df.py:72
  • Required solver change: the regularized configuration contains one stellar DF. Each potential iteration rebuilds its potential-dependent DF, then recomputes density. A multimass version must rebuild all component DFs in the common trial potential, sum their densities, and verify closure for each component. Freezing their initial maps would change the implemented prescription. regularized_df.py:353, regularized_df.py:415
  • Main interface limitation: every count product and kinematic profile currently receives the same projected tracer. Multimass work needs explicit selection-to-component weights; combine surface densities and pressure moments before dividing to obtain dispersions. df_fit.py:130, likelihood.py:453
  • Remnants are prescribed gravity: the regularized branch constructs its Plummer potential directly; changing RemnantPlummer alone would not change this branch. Neither that potential nor the prescribed halo establishes a positive equilibrium remnant/DM DF. regularized_df.py:339

AGAMA supports iterative multicomponent self-consistency. The harder work here is the population/selection likelihood and identifiability, not availability of a potential solver. arXiv:1802.08239

d) Overclaims and cheaper discriminating tests

“Demonstrably wrong” overstates what the photometric budget establishes. The script extrapolates local observed MFs below the detection range and above the turnoff, then assigns inferred WDs to each zone without retention or migration modelling. Its Poisson MF fit does not include completeness uncertainties. The trend is evidence against constant conversion, not a direct measurement of the true total stellar mass profile. build_mass_function.py:183, build_mass_function.py:219

Also check the denominator: the MF catalogue requires both F625W and F814W, whereas the HST count product requires F625W only. The discrepancy matters if F814W availability varies with radius. build_mass_function.py:67, build_count_profiles.py:64

A cheaper scientific test is a two-population tracer/mass separation constrained by corrected radial count ratios, followed by prediction of held-out mass-resolved PM dispersions. That tests segregation using additional observables; tightening the halo bound merely restricts the answer.

Do not calibrate errors by forcing global \(\chi^2/N=1\). The saved fit fails its own data-fit gate, including HST count deviance 98.9 over 20 bins. Separate selection/model errors from measurement errors. summary.json:1204

An odd-\(L_z\) term can fit streaming means while preserving the even DF’s raw second moments. It cannot automatically cure all dispersion residuals. The current moment quadrature explicitly assumes a spherical even DF, so adding rotation requires a compatible moment calculation. positive_df.py:148

1. Verified versus assumed

Verified: the implementation findings above; the saved baseline parameters and objective; nine focused count/mock tests passed with bytecode and pytest caching disabled. Those tests generate synthetic counts using the same density-node averaging, so they do not validate annular integration. best.json:2, tests/test_counts.py:7, tests/test_compact_recovery.py:218

Assumed: the remaining quoted campaign statistics, completeness claims, and astrophysical interpretation. I did not independently reproduce every fit or mock. Twelve point-estimate recovery experiments are not interval-coverage validation. Nothing was modified.

2. Strongest argument against my answer

Even constrained multimass inference may transfer the uncertainty into unobserved low-mass stars, WD retention and the segregation prescription. The measured equipartition is weak. If those uncertainties dominate, corrected single-tracer fits with openly conditional mass-decomposition curves could deliver nearly the same defensible conclusion at substantially lower cost. arXiv:2503.04903

3. What I would check to be sure

  • Independent footprint/completeness-integrated count predictions and catalogue-generated mocks, rather than reused observed nodes.
  • Artificial-star completeness, binary/population effects, and matched photometric/kinematic selections.
  • WD bookkeeping: WDs are currently included in the photometric stellar budget; moving them to a separate component must remove that contribution. build_mass_function.py:234
  • Identical real/mock parameter bounds: defaults currently allow r_s ≤ 150 pc for real fits versus 500 pc for mocks. run_compact_df_recovery.py:293, run_compact_df_recovery.py:419
  • Multistart identifiability and actual interval coverage using segregated, rotating and alternative-remnant truths.
  • Preserve MF inputs and distinct output tags: the script overwrites same-tag outputs and records a plot hash, without recording the raw-catalogue hash. build_mass_function.py:274

docs.title: 1. Executive summary
docs.text:
• Total remnant mass and your added Plummer mass are different quantities. A substantial WD population is already included in a dynamically inferred light-following \(M_\star\). Applying a prior for all WD+NS+BH mass directly to your additional component would double-count some remnants.
  • A canonical IMF gives an old population a remnant mass fraction of roughly 25–40% before preferential stellar escape, depending especially on BH formation and retention. WDs dominate. Dynamical evolution can raise the fraction substantially: published multimass fits include clusters with approximately 50–70% total remnant mass. These are model-dependent population estimates, not universal fractions. Dickson et al. 2023, Baumgardt & Makino 2003.
  • For ω Cen, several independent models support a substantial stellar-mass BH population. Published estimates put approximately 4.5–6% of the total mass in BHs; July–September 2026 preprints obtain approximately 8% and \(\gtrsim7\%\), respectively. This supports a broad prior, rather than adopting one published posterior as a precise constraint. Zocchi et al. 2019, Baumgardt et al. 2019, Dickson et al. 2024, Dickson et al. 2026a,b.
  • Your action-DF component, \(2.7\times10^5\,M_\odot\), is physically sensible. The Jeans component, \(5.4\times10^5\,M_\odot\), is also possible as a mixed non-light-following component, but is more demanding if interpreted entirely as BHs. Its mass is not ruled out by a universal \(5\times10^5\,M_\odot\) ceiling: no such robust ceiling exists.
  • My practical default for your extra component is [ q\equiv M_{\rm rem}/M_\star\sim {\rm HalfNormal}(0.10), \qquad 0\le q\le0.30, ] with a broad scale prior centred around \(a/r_{h,\star}\sim0.3\). These are recommended regularizing priors, not published confidence limits. A separate, broader analysis should allow a mixed WD/faint-star component and alternative formation histories.

docs.title: Mass bookkeeping: the essential distinction
docs.text:
Define [ M_{\rm live}=\text{mass in surviving non-remnant stars}, ] including faint main-sequence stars, and [ M_R=M_{\rm WD}+M_{\rm NS}+M_{\rm BH}. ] For a cluster without a separately counted IMBH or dark-matter component, [ M_{\rm cl}=M_{\rm live}+M_R,\qquad f_R=\frac{M_R}{M_{\rm cl}},\qquad \frac{M_R}{M_{\rm live}}=\frac{f_R}{1-f_R}. ]

Consequently, total remnant fractions of 30%, 50% and 70% correspond to remnant-to-living-star mass ratios of 0.43, 1 and 2.33. Here “living” is a population definition; it does not mean only the bright stars entering a kinematic catalogue.

Your decomposition is instead [ \rho_{\rm tot}(r)=M_\star\,\widehat{\rho}{L}(r) +M}\,\widehat{\rho{P}(r) +M\bullet\delta(\boldsymbol r). ] Because \(M_\star\) includes remnants assigned to the light-following distribution, [ M_{\rm rem}\ne M_R. ]

More precisely, the added component measures mass that the adopted light-following profile does not accommodate. Calling it “remnants” is an interpretation requiring population and spatial-distribution assumptions. This distinction is also explicit in the multicomponent Jeans analysis of Bañares-Hernández et al.: their photometric mass component includes remnants traced by that distribution. Bañares-Hernández et al. 2025, §2.

The physical connection to the IMF is [ M_i(t)=A\int \xi(m)\, m_{i,\rm final}(m,Z,Y)\, P_{i,\rm bound}(m,t)\,dm, ] where the integration domain selects progenitors of remnant type \(i\). The corresponding surviving-star integral fixes \(M_{\rm live}\). The normalization \(A\) is shared: remnant mass cannot be chosen independently of the progenitor population unless the formation and stripping history is also allowed to change.

The retention factor must distinguish natal escape, later dynamical ejection, and tidal stripping. It is generally mass-dependent.

docs.title: Canonical IMF: a numerical baseline
docs.text:
There is no unique “12-Gyr canonical remnant fraction” without specifying the IMF mass limits, IFMR, kick prescription and subsequent escape.

Dickson et al. explicitly state that WDs contribute approximately 30% of the total mass at approximately 10 Gyr for a canonical IMF, before preferential loss of low-mass objects. Dickson et al. 2023, introduction.

For a transparent calculation closer to your requested age, I integrated a Kroupa IMF with:

  • \(dN/dm\propto m^{-1.3}\) from \(0.1\)–\(0.5\,M_\odot\), and \(m^{-2.3}\) from \(0.5\)–\(100\,M_\odot\);
  • turnoff mass \(0.8\,M_\odot\);
  • WD progenitors \(0.8\)–\(8\,M_\odot\), with \(m_{\rm WD}=0.109m+0.394\);
  • \(1.4\,M_\odot\) NSs from \(8\)–\(20\,M_\odot\);
  • an illustrative mean BH mass \(15\,M_\odot\) above \(20\,M_\odot\).

The IMF and empirical WD relation come from Kroupa 2001 and Kalirai et al. 2008. The progenitor boundaries and fixed BH mass are simplifying assumptions, not a modern low-metallicity population-synthesis calculation.

The following numbers are my calculation, not quotations from those papers.

Illustrative population at 12 Gyr WD/total NS/total BH/total All remnants/total WD/living NS/living BH/living All remnants retained; no preferential escape 22.6% 2.0% 8.0% 32.6% 33.5% 2.91% 11.9% 10% NS retention; 50% BH retention 24.0% 0.21% 4.3% 28.4% 33.5% 0.29% 6.0% Same retained remnants, but half the living-star mass removed 37.3% 0.32% 6.6% 44.3% 66.9% 0.58% 11.9%

The final row isolates the denominator effect; actual evolution also removes WDs and BHs.

The useful baseline is therefore:

  • WDs: approximately 20–30% of total retained mass without strong preferential stellar depletion.
  • NSs: approximately a few per cent if all were retained; usually much less than 1% after realistic kicks.
  • BHs: a few per cent, potentially approaching 10% with favourable low-\(Z\) formation and retention.
  • All remnants: approximately 25–40%, with substantial prescription dependence.

A Chabrier IMF provides another canonical baseline, but its precise normalization and single-star/system convention should be specified rather than treating it as numerically identical to Kroupa. Chabrier 2003.

docs.title: What dynamical evolution changes
docs.text:
Preferential stellar loss can raise the remnant fraction without increasing remnant mass. Conversely, BH binary interactions can reduce the BH inventory while heating and expanding the luminous cluster.

Baumgardt & Makino’s stellar-evolution-only fitting formula gives \(f_{\rm WD+NS}\simeq0.283\) at 12 Gyr when evaluated directly. Their dissolving models can become approximately 90% remnants near destruction. However, their IMF ended at \(15\,M_\odot\), and they retained all NSs: this is evidence for the dynamical trend, not a current BH-inclusive population prescription. Baumgardt & Makino 2003, equations 2 and 15, §3.4.

Present-day mass functions support preferential low-mass-star depletion. Sollima & Baumgardt find correlations between MF slopes, relaxation time and dark-remnant fraction; their companion \(N\)-body analysis finds that Kroupa/Chabrier starting IMFs can reproduce the observed MFs. Sollima & Baumgardt 2017, Baumgardt & Sollima 2017.

High BH fractions are also possible without a top-heavy IMF. Gieles et al.’s best Pal 5 model has 22% of its present bound mass in BHs, following loss of approximately 92% of its initial mass. This is a best-fitting evolutionary model, not a confidence interval or a direct BH census. It demonstrates why a universal 10% upper bound is false; it does not establish that ω Cen followed Pal 5’s history. Gieles et al. 2021.

There is an additional complication: BH heating changes WD escape as well as stellar escape. Rostami-Shirazi et al.’s direct simulations find that reproducing the high inferred remnant fractions requires low BH natal kicks in their model grid. Thus “preferential loss always retains every WD” is too simple. Rostami-Shirazi et al. 2025; published online 27 November 2024.

docs.title: Natal kicks and retention
docs.text:
For isolated remnants initially at rest, a Maxwellian kick distribution gives [ P_{\rm ret}(v_{\rm esc},\sigma_k)= {\rm erf}!\left(\frac{v_{\rm esc}}{\sqrt2\sigma_k}\right) -\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{v_{\rm esc}}{\sigma_k} e^{-v_{\rm esc}^2/(2\sigma_k^2)}. ]

Hobbs et al. infer a Maxwellian with one-dimensional dispersion \(265\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}\) for young pulsar birth velocities. This is an observational result for that pulsar sample, not a universal prescription for every NS formation channel. Hobbs et al. 2005.

Calculated retention probabilities under the simplified formula:

Kick dispersion \(v_{\rm esc}=60\) km/s 70 km/s 120 km/s 140 km/s 265 km/s 0.30% 0.48% 2.3% 3.6% 50 km/s 30% 42% 88% 95% 20 km/s 97% 99% approximately 100% approximately 100%

Real calculations must include progenitor velocities, birth positions, binary disruption and binary centre-of-mass recoil.

For NSs, binary evolution and low-kick channels matter enormously. Pfahl et al. find that conventional assumptions give retention below approximately 5% in massive clusters, motivating alternative channels. Modern CMC models distinguish core-collapse NS kicks, \(\sigma=265\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}\), from electron-capture channels, \(\sigma=20\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}\). Pfahl et al. 2002, Kremer et al. 2020, §2.

For BHs, commonly used prescriptions reduce kicks through fallback: [ v_{k,\rm BH}=(1-f_{\rm fallback})\,v_{k,\rm NS}. ] Lower metallicity changes winds, final masses and fallback; the BH mass spectrum and retention must therefore be calculated together. The result depends on the explosion prescription, rather than metallicity supplying a unique retention fraction. Fryer et al. 2012.

For ω Cen, Baumgardt et al. quote a present central escape speed of 63 km/s. Their population calculation uses an initially more massive, smaller cluster and finds that the approximately 4.6% present BH fraction is compatible with several stellar-evolution/kick combinations, after accounting for dynamical ejection. Baumgardt et al. 2019, §4.1.3.

Prior implication: 100% NS retention is an extreme assumption; a fixed 10% NS retention is a useful approximation, not an observation. High BH natal retention in ω Cen is plausible, but “natal retention”, “fraction surviving to today”, and “mass fraction in BHs today” must never be interchanged.

docs.title: Which models impose an IMF-derived inventory?
docs.text:
LIMEPY itself does not impose an IMF. It needs component masses and normalizations; the surrounding population model determines whether these are constrained or free.

Model/application How remnant content enters Hénault-Brunet et al. 2019 Method comparison using mock M4, not a 47 Tuc measurement. Includes flexible remnant-MF and dark-mass parameters; therefore not exclusively an IMF-imposed inventory. The correct citation is MNRAS 483, 1400, not 482. Paper. Hénault-Brunet et al. 2020: 47 Tuc Broken stellar MF with fitted high-mass slope; stellar evolution/IFMR generates remnants. NS retention fixed at 10%; BH retention fitted, with massive BHs removed first to represent dynamical ejection. Paper, §3.2. Dickson et al. 2023/2024 Fitted MF slopes below 0.5, between 0.5–1, and above \(1\,M_\odot\); metallicity-dependent IFMRs; natal-kick prescription and fitted present BH mass-retention parameter. Spatial segregation is tied to component mass through \(s_j\propto m_j^{-\delta}\). Paper I. Zocchi et al. 2019: ω Cen Two-component DF: BHs versus other stars/remnants. Fits BH mass fraction and object-mass ratio; approximately 5% is subsequently checked against population expectations. It is not fixed by an explicit full IMF. Paper, §2.2. Baumgardt et al. 2019: ω Cen Evolved \(N\)-body models: IMF and stellar evolution supply remnants; initial BH retention is varied. BH ejection and segregation then occur dynamically. Paper. CMC/Kremer models IMF, stellar/binary evolution and kicks generate remnants; encounters, escape and tidal evolution determine survival. These are evolutionary predictions conditional on initial conditions and prescriptions. Catalogue paper. Dickson et al. 2026a,b — preprints Couples multimass equilibrium models to clusterBH evolution. Removes the earlier independent BH-retention parameter: dynamical BH depletion is coupled to cluster evolution and energy demand. July preprint, September preprint.

Peuten et al. validate multimass lowered-isothermal models against \(N\)-body populations with different remnant retention. Their success supports the DF machinery; it does not establish a universal remnant abundance. Peuten et al. 2017.

Weatherford et al. instead infer BH populations from the anticorrelation between observable stellar mass segregation and retained BHs, calibrated against simulations. Their 2020 analysis excluded ω Cen because of insufficient radial field coverage. It should not be quoted as an independent ω Cen BH measurement. Weatherford et al. 2018, Weatherford et al. 2020, §4.

docs.title: Verified numerical results for 47 Tuc and ω Cen
docs.text:
47 Tuc is a useful demonstration of WD-rich, BH-poor composition, but is more metal-rich and dynamically different from ω Cen.

Hénault-Brunet et al. infer [ M_{\rm BH}=430^{+386}{-301}\,M\odot ] for 47 Tuc, with quoted errors spanning the 16th–84th posterior percentiles. They also find approximately \(6\times10^4\,M_\odot\) in WDs individually more massive than \(1\,M_\odot\). Thus a small BH fraction does not mean little centrally important remnant mass. Their BH masses depend strongly on the assumed preferential ejection of massive BHs. Hénault-Brunet et al. 2020, §§5.1.2–5.1.3.

For ω Cen:

Study Reported result Zocchi et al. 2019 Anisotropic two-component fit: approximately 4.5%, \(1.35\times10^5\,M_\odot\), in the heavy component; a fitted model value, not a quoted confidence bound. §4.2. Baumgardt et al. 2019 Best-fitting evolved model: approximately 4.6%, \(1.65\times10^5\,M_\odot\), in stellar-mass BHs. §4.1. Dickson et al. 2024 \(f_{\rm BH}=5.9^{+0.2}_{-0.2}\%\), \(M_{\rm BH}=182000^{+5000}_{-6000}\,M_\odot\); total remnant fraction \(50.3^{+0.9}_{-0.3}\%\). All are approximately 68% posterior intervals. Table 1. Dickson et al. 2026a,b July preprint: approximately 8.3% BH mass fraction; September preprint: \(\gtrsim7\%\) under each explored prescription. These are characteristic fitted values, not confidence lower limits. July, §IV.3, September, Fig. 9.

Dickson et al.’s 2024 model also gives 47 Tuc a total remnant fraction \(46.9\pm0.3\%\), despite only approximately 0.046% in BHs. For ω Cen, subtracting its BH contribution leaves approximately 44% in WDs+NSs—my arithmetic, not an independently measured WD fraction. The authors caution that their statistical errors underestimate total uncertainty; mock tests suggest BH-fraction errors can need inflation by approximately 2.5. Dickson et al. 2024, Table 1 and §3.

The 2026 evolution-coupled models explicitly acknowledge additional systematic uncertainty and cannot include an IMBH self-consistently. They therefore update the plausible BH scale without settling the central mass decomposition. Dickson et al. 2026a, §IV.3.

docs.title: White dwarfs: abundant does not mean more concentrated than turnoff stars
docs.text:
The relevant comparison is object mass, not luminosity.

A \(0.55\)–\(0.60\,M_\odot\) WD is:

  • heavier than the typical low-mass main-sequence star;
  • lighter than a normal approximately \(0.8\,M_\odot\) turnoff star;
  • therefore expected, after relaxation, to be more concentrated than low-mass stars but less concentrated than turnoff/giant tracers, other things being equal.

This is an inference from mass-dependent relaxation, not a claim that all WD populations have identical profiles. The illustrative IMF integral above gives a number-weighted mean WD mass \(0.59\,M_\odot\); old massive WDs form an important tail.

There is direct observational support for the change in spatial distribution after mass loss: Heyl et al. measure young WDs diffusing outward through 47 Tuc’s core. Heyl et al. 2015.

ω Cen is additionally complicated by helium-rich populations. Bellini et al. interpret its split bright WD sequence using approximately \(0.55\,M_\odot\) normal-population WDs and approximately \(0.46\,M_\odot\) products associated with helium-rich populations. This is a stellar-evolution interpretation of the sequences, not a global dynamical WD census. Bellini et al. 2013.

For your models: a large WD budget does not automatically justify placing that entire budget in a compact positive Plummer addition to a turnoff-star light profile. Massive WDs, NSs and BHs can supply a concentrated contribution; ordinary low-mass WDs may follow a similar or more extended distribution.

docs.title: Upper limits and unusual formation histories
docs.text:
Remnant mass cannot be arbitrary at fixed IMF, surviving-star normalization and retention history. However, there is no formation-history-independent maximum fraction well below unity: preferential stripping can leave remnant-dominated survivors.

Top-heavy IMFs can increase remnant production, but also increase early mass loss, expansion and disruption. Haghi et al. explicitly model this coupling; one cannot increase the progenitor count while keeping the subsequent cluster history unchanged. Haghi et al. 2020.

The counter-evidence is that Dickson et al.’s multimass fits favour high-mass IMF slopes compatible with canonical values and find no significant metallicity trend. This disfavors using a strongly top-heavy IMF as the default explanation for present GC mass budgets, conditional on their remnant prescriptions. Dickson et al. 2023, §6.1.1.

Multiple populations and a nuclear-cluster origin broaden the possible histories, but do not supply a free mass multiplier:

  • each population has its own surviving stars and remnants;
  • helium changes lifetimes and IFMRs;
  • stripping a host galaxy does not deposit all its remnants in the nucleus;
  • inward transport, capture or cluster mergers require an explicit dynamical history.

My assessment for ω Cen: total remnant fractions around 30–55% are straightforward to entertain; approximately 60–70% is a useful generous sensitivity range. Fractions above that are not mathematically forbidden, but deserve explicit extreme-IMF or selective-stripping models rather than ordinary prior weight. These ranges are my synthesis, not published confidence limits.

Evans et al.’s often-repeated approximately \(5\times10^5\,M_\odot\) remnant allowance is a model-based estimate using selected CMC populations, not a universal upper bound. It also cannot be transferred directly to your extra component without reconciling the luminous-mass definition. Evans, Strigari & Zivick 2022, discussion.

docs.title: Assessment of your two fits
docs.text:
For a Plummer sphere, [ r_{h,\rm rem}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2^{2/3}-1}}=1.305a. ]

Using your inputs:

Quantity Action-DF Jeans \(M_{\rm rem}/M_\star\) 0.090 0.200–0.225 Extra-component fraction of total, including the stated point mass 8.26% 16.45–18.10% \(r_{h,\rm rem}\) 2.87 pc 6.92 pc \(r_{h,\rm rem}/r_{h,\star}\), taking \(r_{h,\star}=10\) pc 0.287 0.692

Thus 16.5% corresponds approximately to the upper end of your Jeans \(M_\star\) range, rather than the whole range.

Action-DF: \(2.7\times10^5\,M_\odot\) at \(a=2.2\) pc is a credible extra remnant component. Its mass and scale are close to the extended central component preferred by Bañares-Hernández et al., who report approximately \(2\)–\(3\times10^5\,M_\odot\) and \(a=1.5\)–2.2 pc at their stated \(3\sigma\) level. Agreement is reassuring but not independent validation if observational inputs overlap. Bañares-Hernández et al. 2025, §6.

Jeans: \(5.4\times10^5\,M_\odot\) is physically possible as a mixed additional component. As BH mass alone, a 16–18% fraction is substantially above existing ω Cen estimates and requires unusually favourable production, retention or stellar depletion. Its broader profile can also absorb radial population/MF changes that a constant light-following \(M/L\) misses. That possibility should be investigated before assigning the whole mass to BHs.

The scale \(r_{h,\rm rem}/r_{h,\star}\simeq0.69\) is not by itself unphysical for a massive BH subsystem. Balanced-evolution theory predicts subsystem size to depend on both BH mass fraction and object-mass ratio; large BH populations need not be extremely compact. Breen & Heggie 2013, equation 4.

docs.title: Priors I would use
docs.text:
Preferred physical formulation: normalize a population model to star counts, sample IMF/IFMR/kick and depletion uncertainties, and predict both the remnant inventory and its spatial distribution. Constrain the light-following \(M/L\) jointly. This prevents an unconstrained exchange between “stellar” and “remnant” mass.

For your present two-component parameterization, I recommend the following explicitly phenomenological priors.

Extra mass: [ q=\frac{M_{\rm rem}}{M_\star} \sim {\rm HalfNormal}(\sigma_q=0.10), \quad 0\le q\le0.30, \qquad M_{\rm rem}=qM_\star. ]

This gives approximately 95% prior probability below \(q\simeq0.19\), after truncation. At \(M_\star=2.4\)–\(3.0\times10^6\,M_\odot\), that is approximately \(4.6\)–\(5.8\times10^5\,M_\odot\). The upper support is \(7.2\)–\(9.0\times10^5\,M_\odot\).

It favours the literature-scale addition while retaining a tail for the Jeans result. The cutoff is a modelling choice, not a physical theorem. For a broader mixed-component sensitivity analysis, use \(\sigma_q=0.15\), \(q_{\max}=0.5\).

Scale, writing \(x=a/r_{h,\star}\): [ \ln x\sim\mathcal N(\ln0.30,\;0.8^2). ]

For a BH-dominated interpretation I would truncate approximately to [ 0.03<x<0.77, ] corresponding to \(r_{h,\rm rem}<r_{h,\star}\). This retains both fitted scales. For a mixed WD/faint-star residual, extend the upper support to \(x\simeq1\), while examining degeneracy with \(M_\star\). The numerical form and bounds are my recommendation, informed by segregation and subsystem physics—not calibrated population constraints.

Total remnant inventory, if separately modelled: a broad starting prior such as [ f_R\sim\mathcal N(0.40,0.12^2),\qquad0.15<f_R<0.70 ] is defensible for sensitivity work on ω Cen. It must be imposed on embedded plus additional remnants together, and cannot substitute for a population model.

A continuous half-normal includes arbitrarily small masses but assigns zero probability to exactly zero. For formal component-existence comparisons, fit a separate \(M_{\rm rem}=0\) model or use a spike-and-slab prior.

docs.title: 3. Disagreements, uncertainties and open questions
docs.text:
1. A large remnant population does not settle the IMBH question. Häberle et al. report central fast stars and an escape-speed lower bound of approximately \(8200\,M_\odot\); their velocity-plus-acceleration analysis gives \(M_\bullet>21100\,M_\odot\) at 99% confidence under their positional assumptions. Häberle et al. 2024. Bañares-Hernández et al.’s combined Jeans/pulsar analysis instead gives \(M_\bullet<6000\,M_\odot\) at stated \(3\sigma\). These are materially inconsistent conditional results, not a combined allowed interval. Bañares-Hernández et al. 2025.

  2. Your \(4.3\times10^4\,M_\odot\) point mass is not forbidden by remnant supply. Evolutionary models starting with IMBH seeds can grow approximately \(5\times10^4\,M_\odot\) objects while matching ω Cen’s broad structure. That establishes a possible formation channel, not a measurement. González Prieto, Rodriguez & Cabrera 2025. The 2026 timing-only preprint gives a much weaker \(M_\bullet<10^5\,M_\odot\) limit at 90% confidence; it does not reproduce the stringent combined-analysis exclusion. Colom i Bernadich et al. 2026, preprint.

  3. Individual BH detections establish existence, not the total inventory. Whitaker et al. report an astrometric companion mass \(4.46^{+1.22}_{-1.01}\,M_\odot\), with 16th–84th percentile errors, assuming a \(0.78\,M_\odot\) visible star. They favour a BH interpretation while discussing rare alternatives. This also shows that low metallicity does not require every retained BH to be massive. Whitaker et al. 2026.

  4. The dominant uncertainties are systematic: BH IFMR and kicks, initial density, primordial binaries, rotation, helium-rich populations, mass-dependent escape, and the translation from observable tracer density to total stellar density. Agreement among models sharing stellar-evolution prescriptions is not fully independent evidence.

  5. Weight of evidence: a WD-rich cluster with a substantial retained BH population is well supported as a physically viable ω Cen model. A uniquely determined BH fraction, a universal \(5\times10^5\,M_\odot\) remnant ceiling, or a settled exclusion/detection of the IMBH is not supported. For your fits, the decisive unresolved issue is how much radial \(M/L\) variation the extra Plummer component is representing.
